Every book is shaped by influences that are not always visible on its pages. This one is no exception.

My deepest gratitude belongs first to God, whose grace has patiently led me from asking questions about life to searching the Scriptures for His answers.

I remain deeply grateful for the life and memory of my late father, Dr Chinwoke Clement Mbadinuju (Odera). His love for God’s Word, commitment to the Foundation and legacy of Christian writing first showed me that serious questions about faith should be explored in language that reaches beyond churches and seminaries to ordinary people seeking honest answers.

I also acknowledge the pastors, teachers, friends and fellow believers whose instruction, conversations and example have helped shape my understanding over the years. Although the arguments and conclusions in this book are my own, they have benefited greatly from the insight, encouragement and companionship of others.

sections.title: Foreword
sections.html:
There are passages of Scripture quoted so often that familiarity has almost silenced them. We know the words, repeat them confidently and yet fail to hear the spiritual force with which they confront us.

Romans 6:23 is one of those passages.

What if “the wages of sin is death” is saying more than believers have considered? What if death is not merely an event at the end of life, but evidence that something has gone profoundly wrong within the human story?

What if sin is deeper than misconduct, redemption greater than moral improvement and eternal life far more than continued existence beyond the grave? And what if the contrast between wages and gift overturns cherished religious assumptions?

Can eternal life remain a gift if human goodness contributes to its purchase? Can grace remain grace if presented as God’s reward for respectable behaviour? If Jesus Christ is central to the answer, why were His Incarnation, obedience, death and Resurrection necessary?

These questions reach into the foundations of what we believe.

In The Wages of Sin, Cheta Mbadinuju examines this familiar verse with the seriousness it deserves. Drawing on lifelong Christian conviction and a career in law and enterprise, he confronts questions no earthly achievement can answer.

He writes neither as a theologian seeking to impress the academy nor as one detached from the ambitions and uncertainties of ordinary life. He writes as a believer compelled to examine afresh a truth he thought he understood.

Readers should therefore expect more than an explanation of death. These pages confront sin and responsibility, judgment and mercy, the humanity and sinlessness of Christ, the mystery of the Cross, the victory of the Resurrection and the meaning of eternal life.

The book brings these truths into everyday life, asking what they mean for people who work, plan, suffer, doubt and face death. Believers may find familiar convictions deepened; secular readers may discover a Christian account of life more searching than they expected.

Neither should remain a spectator. If death is wages and eternal life a gift, what have we earned, what can we receive, and why must it come through Jesus Christ?

Cheta Mbadinuju invites us to hear Romans 6:23 afresh. Read carefully and question honestly, allowing its message to examine your own confidence and call forth your response.

Bishop Paul Nwachukwu Jr
Grace of God Mission Intl.
Onitsha, Anambra State, Nigeria

sections.title: Preface
sections.html:
Some questions arise from curiosity. Others become unavoidable because they concern realities from which none of us can escape.

This book began with one of the latter.

The more I studied the Bible, the clearer it became that the mysteries of human existence cannot be examined apart from God. Questions of identity, suffering, purpose, morality and destiny lead to the One from whom life proceeds and to whom it remains accountable.

Among those questions, one demanded further investigation: Why do we die?

The question appears simple because death is familiar. Every generation encounters it, every family eventually feels its presence, and every human life is lived beneath its possibility. Familiarity is not understanding. We may know that something happens without knowing why it forms part of the human condition at all.

Scripture answers in a single verse:

“For the wages of sin is death; but the gift of God is eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord.” Romans 6:23

Many Christians know the verse by heart, yet familiarity can dull its force. Wages are earned; a gift is freely given. Death belongs to the first, eternal life belongs to the second, and between them stands Jesus Christ.

The verse grows more searching the closer it is examined. What does it mean for death to be the wages of sin? Is Paul merely describing the inevitable end of human life, or is he revealing something about our relationship with God and the condition into which humanity has fallen?

And what of the other half of the verse? If death is earned and eternal life is given, what accounts for the difference? Why should the destiny of humanity turn on a distinction between what is deserved and what is freely bestowed?

Beneath the ordinary certainty that everyone dies lies a less ordinary question: by what right does death lay claim to us? And beyond our desire to escape it stands a greater one: whether the life we struggle to preserve is all that human existence was meant to be.

These are not minor theological puzzles. They touch the foundations of the Christian faith and the fears, losses and expectations of ordinary human life. They call for answers that are faithful to Scripture and clear enough to be understood beyond the walls of a seminary.

I come to this enquiry as a practising lawyer, not a professional theologian. I do not offer that as an excuse for imprecision. It explains my method.

Legal practice teaches the discipline of identifying the precise question, examining the evidence, distinguishing assertion from proof, testing apparent contradictions and resisting conclusions that go beyond what the evidence can sustain. It also teaches that seemingly simple propositions often conceal complexities that emerge only when their underlying assumptions are tested.

I have brought that discipline to this enquiry, with Scripture as its governing authority. My approach has been to examine its testimony concerning sin, death and redemption, read related passages in their proper contexts and distinguish what the Bible expressly reveals from what we may have come to assume. Apparent difficulties will not be avoided. Necessary distinctions will not be flattened into convenient simplicity. I have tried neither to force a conclusion on Scripture nor to explain away its mysteries.

No single book can resolve every theological controversy connected with this subject. Faithful Christians have differed over aspects of original sin, atonement, salvation and the events surrounding the end of the age. Where such disagreements arise, I seek to engage them fairly without allowing particular debates to obscure the central testimony of Scripture.

The purpose of this enquiry is narrower: to trace the biblical account from the entrance of sin and death, through the unfolding promise of redemption, to its fulfilment in the Incarnation, Cross and Resurrection of Jesus Christ. The book then examines the gift of eternal life, its implications for how we live and the promised abolition of death.

At the heart of this enquiry stands a Person, not a philosophy or a human scheme for escaping mortality. Christianity claims that, through Jesus Christ, God entered human history to confront a condition humanity could not overcome by its own efforts. That claim can be tested.

I write for more than theologians and ministers. This book is for Christians who want a clearer grasp of what they believe, and for readers who remain uncertain, sceptical or simply curious about what Christianity claims concerning humanity’s oldest enemy.

I do not presume that every reader accepts the authority of the Bible. I ask only that Scripture’s testimony be heard fairly and examined as a whole. A claim is not beyond scrutiny because it is familiar. Nor should it be dismissed unexamined because it is religious.

This book, however, is more than an intellectual enquiry. If Scripture speaks truly, its implications extend far beyond what awaits us after death. Eternal life is not merely a promise concerning the future; it bears upon our relationship with God, our understanding of ourselves, our obligations towards others and the meaning and purpose of our lives today.

Before examining these claims, we should begin closer to home, with an ordinary day and the assumptions that carry us through it. The Prologue begins there.

Unless otherwise indicated, all Scripture quotations in this book are taken from the King James Version of the Holy Bible.

sections.title: Prologue
sections.subtitle: The Quest for a Longer Life
sections.html:
I woke up today with a plan.

There were messages to answer, decisions to make and responsibilities requiring my attention. Some concerned the day before me; others depended upon events expected weeks or months from now.

That is how most of us live. We organise our affairs around the reasonable expectation that life will continue. We schedule meetings, begin projects, make investments, book journeys and prepare our children for futures we hope to witness.

Planning is necessary. It allows families, businesses and societies to function. Within every plan, however, lies an assumption we seldom examine: that we will remain alive long enough to carry it out.

Few people begin an ordinary morning expecting it to be their last. We may pray for protection and take sensible precautions, but we generally expect to return home, sleep and resume our activities the following day.

Sometimes that expectation is interrupted.

A person may leave home for work and never return. Another may attend a routine medical examination and receive a diagnosis that changes the meaning of every remaining day. For some, the end comes suddenly; for others, illness makes its approach visible long before it arrives.

Sudden death denies families the chance to prepare. Prolonged illness makes them watch someone they love weaken under a condition they are powerless to reverse.

When death enters a family, it also brings practical demands that seem strangely indifferent to grief. Calls must be made, relatives informed, documents obtained and burial arrangements discussed. Decisions are required while the mind is still struggling to accept what has happened.

The passing of my late father brought that reality painfully close to me. A man whose voice, convictions and presence had helped shape my understanding of life was no longer there. So much of what he had given me remained, but I could no longer turn to him as I tried to make sense of life without him.

Public ceremonies eventually ended, visitors returned home and ordinary responsibilities resumed. Bereavement did not conclude with the burial. It continued in quieter moments: a photograph, a remembered expression, an unanswered question or the instinct to make a telephone call that could no longer be made.

Loss makes mortality personal. It removes death from the safety of abstraction and places it within the family, where explanations cannot replace the person whose absence we feel.

Perhaps our awareness of that possibility explains part of humanity’s persistent quest for longer life.

We exercise, improve our diets, monitor our health and seek treatment when needed. Life is precious, and attention to health is part of its proper stewardship. Medical science has prevented immense suffering, controlled once-fatal diseases and added years to countless lives.

Medicine can also investigate death with great precision. A post-mortem examination may identify the disease, injury or organ failure that ended a particular life. Its findings can bring clarity to a family, assist justice and help prevent similar deaths.

Identifying the immediate cause, however, does not settle every question raised by the event.

When a medical examination identifies heart disease, cancer, infection or traumatic injury as the cause of death, it explains the physical circumstances. It tells us how an individual died. It cannot say why anyone must.

Ageing reminds us of our mortality even in the absence of illness. When I compare recent photographs with those taken during my MBA at Buckingham or my matriculation at the University of Nigeria, the passage of time is unmistakable. The man is recognisably the same, but the years have left their marks on his face and body.

There was no single moment when it happened. The years accumulated through ordinary days until the distance between the younger man in those photographs and the man now studying them became impossible to overlook.

Every birthday carries this double meaning. We celebrate the blessing of another year, even as we acknowledge time we can never reclaim. The number rises, but the years remaining are never guaranteed.

Humanity has long sought to slow that passage. Ancient civilisations imagined fountains of youth and elixirs of immortality; modern science investigates genes, cells and the biological processes of ageing. The methods have changed, but the desire is the same.

We want more time.

We want to see children mature, ambitions fulfilled and labour rewarded. We want another conversation with those we love, another opportunity to repair what has gone wrong and another year to complete what remains unfinished.

There is nothing shameful about that desire. The longing to preserve life is natural, and we owe a debt to the advances that serve it. But extending life is not escaping death. Medicine may postpone the grave; it has not abolished it.

Scripture enters the discussion by connecting humanity’s mortality with a rupture that is both moral and spiritual. Paul’s sentence in Romans 6:23 does not begin with biology or the length of our years. It begins with sin.

That is an uncomfortable place to begin. It takes death out of the category of misfortune and puts it in the category of consequence.

How did that connection arise, and how does it explain the death of people whose lives are marked by kindness, integrity and love?

If humanity cannot escape death, what hope does Scripture offer, and why does it centre on Jesus Christ? What makes His death and Resurrection different from every other death in history, and what is the eternal life Paul calls God’s gift?

One question presses harder. Christians still fall ill, endure suffering, grieve and die. If Christ has conquered death, why do those who receive His gift remain subject to it? What has His victory accomplished, and what remains to be fulfilled?

We began with the pursuit of longer life. The question now before us lies beyond the reach of medicine. Before we can understand what it means to overcome death, we must understand where death came from.

That is where the enquiry begins.

sections.title: Part I
sections.subtitle: The Mortal Question
sections.html:
“Wherefore, as by one man sin entered into the world, and death by sin; and so death passed upon all men, for that all have sinned.” Romans 5:12

The Apostle Paul’s declaration places every grave within a larger human story. Death is familiar to every generation, but familiarity does not explain why it belongs to the human condition.

Paul traces its entrance to one man and connects it with sin. How should we understand that claim? What happened in Eden, and why should its consequences reach people who were not there?

His words also require us to consider what came before. What was humanity’s original condition, and what changed when Adam and Eve disobeyed God? If death entered through sin, what does Scripture mean by death?

Then comes Paul’s troubling conclusion: “for that all have sinned.” How does Adam’s disobedience relate to the lives of those who followed him? Where does an inherited human condition meet each person’s responsibility for his or her own actions?

These questions lead towards the first half of the verse that governs this book:

“For the wages of sin is death.” Romans 6:23

Before we can understand the gift Paul announces, we must examine the condition to which it speaks.

Part I begins with the fact before us, returns to Eden and then considers the meaning of Paul’s verdict. The investigation starts where every reader can recognise the evidence: with the inevitability of death.

sections.title: The Inevitability of Death
sections.html:
The Universal Human Condition

Some realities are so familiar that we cease to regard them as questions.

Mortality is one of them. Human beings are born, grow, age and eventually die. The pattern seems so settled that death is treated as self-explanatory.

We differ in nationality, culture, beliefs, abilities and circumstances. Some enjoy wealth, influence and opportunity; others face deprivation or insecurity. These differences shape our lives, but none exempts us from death.

Wealth may provide excellent medical care, education enlarge understanding and moral character leave an honourable legacy. Such advantages matter. They cannot secure permanent life. Kings and labourers eventually return to the same earth.

Nor is every life equal in duration. One person dies in infancy, another in youth and another after many decades. The differences are considerable, but they occur within the same mortal order.

In law, as in other fields of enquiry, a recurring outcome invites investigation. When substantially the same result appears across different persons, places and circumstances, we ask whether the cases point towards a common underlying condition. Mortality presents that kind of evidence.

One qualification follows. Mortality governs the human race, but not every individual must undergo physical death. Scripture itself forbids an exceptionless claim.

The Rule and the Exceptions

The Old Testament records two extraordinary exceptions.

Of Enoch it says:

“And Enoch walked with God: and he was not; for God took him.” Genesis 5:24

The New Testament makes the meaning explicit:

“By faith Enoch was translated that he should not see death.” Hebrews 11:5

Enoch did not undergo the ordinary experience of physical death. God took him.

Elijah provides a second example. At the conclusion of his earthly ministry, Scripture records:

“And Elijah went up by a whirlwind into heaven.” 2 Kings 2:11

The New Testament extends the point beyond these individuals. Writing of believers alive at the return of Jesus Christ, Paul declares:

“We shall not all sleep, but we shall all be changed.” 1 Corinthians 15:51

In another letter, he describes those who remain alive at that event:

“Then we which are alive and remain shall be caught up together with them in the clouds, to meet the Lord in the air.” 1 Thessalonians 4:17

Scripture therefore anticipates believers who will be transformed at Christ’s return without first entering the grave. All require transformation; not all must first die.

These accounts also show that death does not operate independently of God. Enoch’s translation, Elijah’s departure and the promised transformation of living believers reveal His authority over mortality.

Our question is more precise than whether God can prevent a particular person from dying. Scripture says He can. We must ask why mortality reigns over us at all.

The exceptions do not explain that reign, but they prevent us from treating it as a necessity beyond divine power.

What Science Can Explain

Few achievements of modern civilisation are as admirable as the progress of science and medicine.

Diseases that once devastated populations can now be prevented, controlled or treated. Surgery restores functions earlier generations could not have hoped to recover, while medical imaging reveals conditions hidden within the body. Research into genetics, infection and cellular behaviour continues to improve the preservation of life.

These achievements relieve suffering and give people time with those they love. Scientific explanation is indispensable to understanding the physical conditions in which we live and the processes by which we die.

Biology investigates ageing, cellular deterioration and organ failure. Physicians diagnose illness, while pathologists identify the physical causes of particular deaths. Scientific enquiry also examines the history of living organisms and the development of the processes that make them mortal.

Its contribution therefore extends beyond explaining an individual death. It can identify patterns, reconstruct aspects of biological history and test explanations against physical evidence.

The question pursued in this book has another dimension. Does human mortality bear a meaning within our relationship with God? Does Scripture describe it as part of a moral history in which command, rebellion and judgment matter?

An account of biological processes does not, by itself, settle those questions.

The distinction is familiar in legal practice. A forensic pathologist may establish the injury that caused death. Further evidence may be required to determine how it occurred, who was responsible and what intention accompanied the act.

The medical finding remains essential. Its contribution is better understood when we recognise the particular question it answers.

The comparison helps us distinguish physical explanation from questions of responsibility and meaning. Science can investigate the processes that make bodies mortal; its methods alone do not establish whether human mortality also represents divine judgment.

Recognising that distinction does justice to both enquiries. The relief of suffering remains valuable whether or not a patient shares the physician’s beliefs. The theological question remains worth examining even when the physical cause of death is fully understood.

The present enquiry asks what Scripture claims about humanity’s mortal condition and what grounds it gives for that claim. It looks at the relationship between death and humanity’s estrangement from its Creator.

The Boundary of Observation

Observation gives us knowledge of the world we encounter. Through physical evidence, scientific enquiry can also reconstruct aspects of a past no living observer witnessed. The absence of an eyewitness does not make historical investigation impossible.

Questions about divine intention and judgment lie beyond what physical evidence can settle. Evidence may show what happened to a body or how a biological process developed, but it cannot by itself identify an event as an act of God’s judgment.

To understand such a claim, we must examine the revelation through which it is made. Scripture presents mortality within an account of God’s dealings with humanity, and that account must be heard on its own terms.

This is not a proposal to assign whatever science leaves unexplained to God. Such reasoning would make divine action a temporary answer to gaps in human knowledge, withdrawn whenever a physical explanation became available.

The biblical claim concerns more than an unanswered biological question. It identifies a relationship between humanity and its Creator, describes its rupture and connects death with what occurred.

One need not accept that account in advance to understand the enquiry. We can first ask what Scripture says, distinguish its declarations from interpretations added to them, and examine whether the argument drawn from its passages is coherent.

In legal terms, the Bible enters this investigation as testimony concerning events, purposes and relationships. Its authority cannot be assumed on behalf of every reader, but its claim must be heard accurately before it is assessed.

Its account begins with life.

When Revelation Enters the Enquiry

The opening chapter of Genesis describes a world brought into existence by divine command and repeatedly pronounced good. Humanity appears as God’s deliberate work, made in His image and entrusted with responsibility within His creation.

Before Scripture records the first human death, it records a warning. God places the man in the Garden and gives him a command with its consequence:

“But of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, thou shalt not eat of it: for in the day that thou eatest thereof thou shalt surely die.” Genesis 2:17

This is the first direct reference to human death in the biblical narrative. Death appears as the consequence attached to disobedience.

A boundary has been established. Adam is told what he must not do and what will follow if he does it. The warning places death within the relationship between the creature and the Creator who gives the command.

The boundary was crossed. Eve ate of the forbidden fruit and gave it to Adam, who ate also.

At this point, we must resist moving faster than the narrative permits.

What did God mean by “thou shalt surely die”? Adam did not die physically that day. How was the warning fulfilled, and how does Scripture connect alienation from God, mortality and bodily death?

Then there is the act itself. Why should eating from a forbidden tree carry so grave a consequence? Was the offence located in the fruit’s properties, or in the rejection of God’s authority expressed through taking it?

Quoting the warning cannot answer these questions by itself.

For now, one finding stands. Scripture’s first reference to human death connects it with disobedience. The narrative gives mortality a moral and relational setting.

Paul later interprets that history:

“Wherefore, as by one man sin entered into the world, and death by sin; and so death passed upon all men, for that all have sinned.” Romans 5:12

His sequence is deliberate: sin entered; death followed. He connects the act of one man with a condition extending throughout humanity.

Paul interprets death within the history of humanity’s relationship with God. The biological processes remain real; his claim concerns the larger condition in which they operate.

If death entered through sin, we must understand what happened in Eden before considering how its consequences reached those who came afterwards.

The Question That Takes Us to Eden

Human experience teaches us that death is an unavoidable reality of life. Scripture, however, presents a more unsettling proposition: that humanity’s mortal condition is bound to a rupture in its relationship with God.

Such a claim deserves careful examination, particularly for readers who do not already accept biblical authority. Quoting Scripture establishes what it declares, but understanding why it connects death with human rebellion requires us to examine the account in which that connection first emerges.

That account takes us to a world before human disobedience, where God provided for humanity, established the boundaries of human freedom and warned of consequences whose significance would extend far beyond the first generation.

What occurred in that relationship between Creator and creation that would leave death casting its shadow over every human life?

To investigate that question, we must return to where the biblical account begins: the Garden of Eden.

sections.title: The Day Death Entered the World
sections.html:
Eden Before the Fall: God’s Original Design

The Bible’s account of death takes us beyond the fact that living bodies cease to function. It places death within a moral and relational history that begins in Eden.

What happened there that was serious enough to introduce death into the human story?

To answer that question, Scripture takes us to humanity before its first recorded bereavement. Before death became our common inheritance, Genesis describes life received from God within His generous provision. To understand what humanity lost, we must first consider what it possessed.

The opening chapters present a creation repeatedly pronounced good. Within it, God prepares a garden, provides food and gives the man meaningful work. The account begins with provision and responsibility rather than estrangement and judgment.

Humanity appears as the deliberate work of God, fashioned in His image and entrusted with a place within His creation. Adam receives life from his Creator and hears Him speak.

His story therefore begins with favour. He did not discover God through a prolonged search or establish his identity through achievement. God made Himself known and gave Adam a calling before Adam had done anything to earn it.

Such a beginning is difficult to imagine from within our experience. We know relationships in which trust can fail, promises can be broken and love can be wounded. Even our happiest moments cannot guarantee freedom from loss.

Genesis presents an important contrast: the man and woman were naked without shame. Hiding and fear enter the narrative after disobedience, when their response to God’s presence changes.

One qualification is necessary. The account does not require us to imagine Adam possessing an independent immortality inherent within himself. His life, like every other good he received, remained dependent upon God.

Genesis 3 makes that dependence clear. After the Fall, God bars access to the Tree of Life lest man eat and live forever in his fallen condition.

The Tree of Life therefore has a significant place in the account of continuing life. Humanity is not presented as a self-sustaining source of existence. Adam’s life was received, and its continuation could not be separated from God’s provision.

These details establish the relationship within which the command was given. Genesis 3 concerns more than a forbidden object; it records humanity’s response to the God who had already given life, provision and responsibility.

Humanity did not begin estranged from Him. Before disobedience, there was fellowship; before judgment, there was generosity. The command was given to people who had reason to trust the One who spoke.

The gravity of Adam and Eve’s act must therefore be considered within that relationship.

The Command and the Counterclaim

Scripture records God’s command with remarkable simplicity:

“And the LORD God commanded the man, saying, Of every tree of the garden thou mayest freely eat: But of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, thou shalt not eat of it: for in the day that thou eatest thereof thou shalt surely die.” Genesis 2:16–17

The generosity preceding the prohibition deserves attention. Adam was not placed in deprivation and denied the means of living. The boundary stood within abundant provision.

The command presented a profound question of trust. Would man receive life on the terms established by the God who gave it, or claim authority to determine those terms for himself?

Its warning was equally clear: disobedience would bring death. At this point in the narrative, however, death remained a warning rather than a recorded human experience.

No child had buried a parent, and no mother had mourned a son. The words “thou shalt surely die” described a consequence Adam had not encountered.

The warning required him to trust God concerning something beyond his experience. Would the Creator’s word be sufficient, or would another account of reality prove more attractive?

Genesis introduces the competing voice:

“Now the serpent was more subtil than any beast of the field which the LORD God had made. And he said unto the woman, Yea, hath God said, Ye shall not eat of every tree of the garden?” Genesis 3:1

The serpent began with a question about what God had said. Its wording placed the prohibition at the centre of attention, obscuring the freedom within which it stood.

The first challenge was to confidence in God’s Word. Eve was drawn into a conversation in which His command could be reconsidered through another voice.

The conversation then moved from His words to His character:

“And the serpent said unto the woman, Ye shall not surely die: For God doth know that in the day ye eat thereof, then your eyes shall be opened, and ye shall be as gods, knowing good and evil.” Genesis 3:4–5

The contradiction was explicit. God had said, “Thou shalt surely die.” The serpent replied, “Ye shall not surely die.” Their claims could not both be trusted.

Eve faced competing accounts of the consequence before her. Whose word would govern her choice?

The serpent also placed God’s motive under suspicion. The Creator who had provided the garden was portrayed as withholding something desirable. Once the prohibition appeared to conceal an advantage, disobedience could begin to resemble liberation.

This is one of Genesis 3’s enduring insights into temptation. Sin does not always begin by making evil appear good. Sometimes it begins by making God appear less good.

When His wisdom seems unnecessarily restrictive, His commands become negotiable. When His generosity is doubted, taking matters into our own hands begins to seem reasonable. Human judgment assumes the right to sit in review over divine revelation.

Before the fruit was taken, the conversation had already supplied reasons to distrust the One who forbade it.

The Fall: The Heart Turns Before the Hand

Genesis records the decisive moment:

“And when the woman saw that the tree was good for food, and that it was pleasant to the eyes, and a tree to be desired to make one wise, she took of the fruit thereof, and did eat, and gave also unto her husband with her; and he did eat.” Genesis 3:6

The account records no immediate physical collapse. A woman takes the fruit, eats and gives it to a man who eats also. Within the biblical narrative, few acts carry greater consequence.

The offence cannot be understood simply by describing the movement of their hands. The act occurred after God’s warning had been contradicted and the forbidden tree presented as a source of desirable wisdom.

Eve saw the tree differently. Its appeal was now weighed against the command, and she took what God had forbidden. The outward act disclosed a decision about whose word deserved trust.

Humanity’s first sin was more than reaching towards a tree. It was a turning away from the authority of the God who had given life.

Sin expresses itself through actions, but those actions reveal an underlying relationship to God. Here, the creature’s judgment displaced the Creator’s command.

The claim to autonomy need not take the form of openly denying God’s existence. It can appear when His will is known but treated as something we may set aside. The creature assumes a jurisdiction that belongs to the Creator.

In legal enquiry, an act matters alongside the intention and circumstances that give it significance. Genesis supplies a command, a counterclaim and a deliberate crossing of the boundary. Adam and Eve did more than breach an unexplained technical rule.

A modern reader may still ask why eating from a tree should have consequences so severe. The question is reasonable, but the seriousness of an act cannot always be measured by its physical size.

A signature consists of ink on paper, yet may transfer an estate. A few spoken words can create an obligation or pronounce a judgment. Their significance lies in the authority and relationship within which they operate.

So it was in Eden. The fruit’s significance cannot be confined to its physical properties. God had established the boundary, and taking the fruit expressed a refusal to receive life under His authority.

Humanity acted as though God’s provision could be enjoyed while His command was disregarded. The consequences would disclose the depth of that error.

Shame, Fear and Blame

The serpent had promised opened eyes and greater wisdom. Their eyes were indeed opened, but discovery brought no fulfilment:

“And the eyes of them both were opened, and they knew that they were naked; and they sewed fig leaves together, and made themselves aprons.” Genesis 3:7

The outcome differed from the promise. Instead of the anticipated advantage, the narrative first records awareness of nakedness and an attempt to cover it.

Genesis had described them as naked and unashamed. Now concealment enters their experience. The hands that reached for the fruit reach for fig leaves.

Their first recorded response was self-covering. Their next response disclosed how profoundly their relationship with God had changed:

“And they heard the voice of the LORD God walking in the garden in the cool of the day: and Adam and his wife hid themselves from the presence of the LORD God amongst the trees of the garden.” Genesis 3:8

The people to whom God had given life now hid from Him. The narrative gives no suggestion that He had become less holy or less trustworthy. Their disobedience had changed the way they encountered His presence.

God called to Adam: “Where art thou?” Genesis 3:9

The question draws Adam into an answer. It exposes more than his location; it brings his changed condition into the open.

Adam replied: “I heard thy voice in the garden, and I was afraid, because I was naked; and I hid myself.” Genesis 3:10

His words describe fear and concealment where the preceding account had described unashamed life. The rupture is visible before a human grave appears.

Adam remained physically alive, but this does not make God’s warning empty. Alienation had begun, and the judgment soon pronounced would make his eventual return to dust explicit.

Genesis itself does not call Adam’s hiding “spiritual death.” Later Scripture uses death-language for people still living in estrangement from God, helping us understand the relationship between alienation and mortality. These realities must remain distinguishable even as we examine their connection.

The rupture also became visible between the man and woman. When God asked whether Adam had eaten from the forbidden tree, he replied:

“The woman whom thou gavest to be with me, she gave me of the tree, and I did eat.” Genesis 3:12

The woman previously received as God’s provision now appeared in Adam’s defence. His words implicated both her and the God who had given her to him.

Responsibility moved outward. Adam pointed to the woman; the woman pointed to the serpent. Both acknowledged eating, but their explanations directed attention towards someone else.

Distrust had become disobedience, followed by concealment and blame. The relationship with God was wounded, and the relationship between the man and woman now bore its effects.

The next generation would disclose a more violent expression of human wrongdoing. Genesis 4 records Cain killing Abel. What began with taking forbidden fruit would be followed by the taking of a brother’s life.

Judgment would now declare the seriousness of the rebellion already before us.

Judgment, Mercy and Exile

God’s judgment extends into everyday human existence. Childbearing becomes marked by sorrow, labour by toil and the ground by thorns and thistles. Life, still sustained by His provision, will now unfold amid hardship.

The sentence upon Adam reaches its terrible conclusion:

“In the sweat of thy face shalt thou eat bread, till thou return unto the ground; for out of it wast thou taken: for dust thou art, and unto dust shalt thou return.” Genesis 3:19

The warning of Genesis 2 has become the judgment of Genesis 3. “Thou shalt surely die” is followed by “unto dust shalt thou return.”

The narrative places human death within a moral sequence: command, distrust, rebellion and judgment. Adam’s bodily end is expressly connected with the sentence pronounced after his disobedience.

No grave appears yet, but the return to dust has been declared. In the next chapter, Cain’s killing of Abel will bring death into the family through violence.

Judgment, however, is not the only word spoken in Eden. In addressing the serpent, God declares:

“And I will put enmity between thee and the woman, and between thy seed and her seed; it shall bruise thy head, and thou shalt bruise his heel.” Genesis 3:15

The words announce conflict and injury on both sides. Read within Scripture’s unfolding account, they also point towards the overcoming of the deceiver.

Genesis does not disclose every stage of that fulfilment. The fuller Christian understanding of the promise depends upon what later Scripture reveals. Its development belongs to the enquiry ahead.

God also clothes the man and woman:

“Unto Adam also and to his wife did the LORD God make coats of skins, and clothed them.” Genesis 3:21

We should not force into this verse everything later Scripture teaches about sacrifice and atonement. Genesis records God’s provision of clothing without explaining it in those terms.

The contrast remains significant. Adam and Eve had attempted to cover themselves; God clothed them. His judgment did not mean that every expression of His care had ceased.

They were then expelled:

“Therefore the LORD God sent him forth from the garden of Eden, to till the ground from whence he was taken.” Genesis 3:23

The expulsion has relational significance as well as geographical consequence. Humanity leaves the place where God’s provision had been received before rebellion. Access to the Tree of Life is barred.

The narrative gives the reason: man must not take from it and live forever in his fallen condition. Continuing life could no longer be approached as though disobedience had changed nothing.

Sin promised advantage while concealing the cost of disobedience. Adam and Eve left Eden bearing shame, toil and the sentence of returning to dust.

They did not leave without hope. Alongside judgment, God had spoken of the serpent’s defeat and supplied clothing for those who had disobeyed Him.

Creation Under Corruption

The consequences of Eden did not end at the Garden’s boundary. The ground is cursed because of Adam, and humanity’s work within creation becomes burdened by frustration.

This raises a further question. If human death entered through Adam’s sin, why do animals also die? They did not eat from the forbidden tree and cannot be said to have earned sin’s wages through moral rebellion comparable to ours.

The distinction matters. Paul’s argument concerning Adam is directed to humanity: sin entered through one man, death entered through sin and death passed upon mankind. It does not say that every creature dies because it personally sinned.

Scripture nevertheless connects creation’s present suffering with the wider condition from which redemption will deliver it. Paul writes:

“For we know that the whole creation groaneth and travaileth in pain together until now.” Romans 8:22

Creation shares in corruption without being described as morally guilty alongside Adam. Animals inhabit the world in which fallen humanity lives, but their mortality and the judgment upon human rebellion are not identical propositions.

Human death has a moral and spiritual significance within the biblical account. Humanity is answerable to the Creator whose command was broken. Animal suffering cannot simply be explained by assigning animals the same responsibility.

Scripture does not supply a detailed chronology of every form of creaturely death. Nor does it explain every relationship between Adam’s sin, animal mortality and suffering throughout the natural world.

That limitation should be acknowledged. The passages establish creation’s bondage to corruption without answering every question about when or how each aspect of its present condition arose.

Paul also directs attention beyond that condition:

“Because the creature itself also shall be delivered from the bondage of corruption into the glorious liberty of the children of God.” Romans 8:21

Creation’s groaning is accompanied by hope. God’s purpose reaches beyond the redemption of human beings to the world they inhabit.

The consequences of humanity’s rebellion extend into creation. The promise of restoration also reaches beyond humanity alone.

From Adam to Every Generation

We can now return to the question with which this chapter began. What happened in Eden that introduced death into the human story?

The issue went beyond eating fruit. Humanity distrusted God’s word and disobeyed His command, rejecting His authority within a relationship sustained by His provision.

Its consequences revealed the depth of the rupture. Shame replaced unashamed openness, hiding followed disobedience, and blame entered the relationship between the man and woman. Judgment brought toil, expulsion and the declared return to dust.

Genesis therefore presents the Fall as a change in humanity’s relationship with God. The people He had made remained His creatures, but their life could no longer continue as though the command had been kept.

The account describes our world: we bear God’s image while resisting Him, seek closeness while wounding one another, and desire life while remaining mortal. Eden gives these realities a history.

Another question now requires attention. Adam and Eve disobeyed before any of us were born. Why should their act explain our condition, and how can Paul move from one man’s rebellion to death passing upon all?

Individual imitation cannot, by itself, explain the whole argument. Paul describes sin and death as reigning within humanity, while Scripture continues to hold people responsible for their own conduct.

We must therefore examine how the inherited condition relates to personal guilt. What belongs to humanity through Adam, and what does each person add through his or her own choices?

The enquiry moves from the first disobedience to its reach across generations. Those questions bring us to the sentence at the centre of this book:

“The wages of sin is death.” Romans 6:23

sections.title: The Wages of Sin
sections.html:
The Wages and the Gift

The rupture in Eden did not end with those who first experienced it. Sin, alienation and mortality became part of the human story across generations. How did one man’s act reach so far beyond his own life?

That question returns us to the declaration with which Part I began:

“Wherefore, as by one man sin entered into the world, and death by sin; and so death passed upon all men, for that all have sinned.” Romans 5:12

Genesis records the entrance of sin and death. Paul considers how Adam’s act came to define the condition in which subsequent generations live.

His argument leads us to this book’s governing verse:

“For the wages of sin is death; but the gift of God is eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord.” Romans 6:23

This declaration belongs within Paul’s account of Adam, judgment and death’s reign. Its immediate setting also matters: Romans 6 examines the dominion of sin and the changed allegiance of those who belong to Christ.

The sentence contains two outcomes governed by different principles. Death is described as wages; eternal life as a gift. One is connected to sin, the other proceeds from God through Jesus Christ.

Before we consider the gift, we must understand the wages.

A wage is payment due for service rendered. An employee receives it because work has been performed, not because the employer has chosen to make an unrelated act of generosity. Paul’s language carries that sense of something earned and owed.

Throughout Romans 6, he speaks of masters, servants and obedience:

“Know ye not, that to whom ye yield yourselves servants to obey, his servants ye are to whom ye obey; whether of sin unto death, or of obedience unto righteousness?” Romans 6:16

Sin appears as more than occasional misconduct. Paul describes it as a master whose service establishes an allegiance and leads towards an outcome.

He asks those who had served it: “What fruit had ye then in those things whereof ye are now ashamed? for the end of those things is death.” Romans 6:21

Sin presents itself as freedom from God, but those who yield to it become its servants. Its promise of autonomy produces bondage. Life pursued on humanity’s own terms ends in death.

Eden had already exposed that deception. Taking what God forbade appeared to offer an advantage; the act instead brought judgment and exile. Paul now describes the dominion within which that rebellion continued.

Death is the wage with which sin finally pays its servants. Eternal life, however, is not a better payment awarded to those whose conduct becomes sufficiently impressive. It is “the gift of God.”

Wages arise from service rendered; the gift proceeds from the Giver’s generosity. Paul contrasts what sin pays with what God gives.

We must therefore ask what death signifies within this argument. How does service to sin relate to the mortal condition shared by humanity?

What Does Paul Mean by Death?

Scripture uses the language of death in more than one setting. Its most visible expression is bodily: life ceases, a person’s earthly presence is withdrawn and those who remain encounter the reality of loss.

Hebrews states the ordinary human course with solemn economy:

“And as it is appointed unto men once to die, but after this the judgment.” Hebrews 9:27

This was one of my late father’s favourite verses of admonition. He used it to remind those who heard him that time is limited, life is accountable and death does not end our answerability to God.

The verse describes the ordinary course without denying the exceptional acts of divine sovereignty already considered. It also directs attention beyond the grave: death is followed by judgment.

Elsewhere, people who remain physically alive are described as dead. Paul writes of the former condition of believers in Ephesus:

“And you hath he quickened, who were dead in trespasses and sins.” Ephesians 2:1

The following verse describes their activity:

“Wherein in time past ye walked according to the course of this world…” Ephesians 2:2

They were dead, and still they walked. They thought, desired, acted and participated in society. Paul was describing a condition that bodily activity did not remove.

His language concerns their life in sin, estranged from God. Natural existence continued, but the fellowship for which humanity was created had been broken.

Jesus uses a related image in the parable of the lost son:

“For this my son was dead, and is alive again; he was lost, and is found.” Luke 15:24

The son had returned from estrangement, not from a physical grave. His father describes the restored relationship through the contrast between death and life.

These passages distinguish bodily existence from fellowship with God. They also help us consider Eden, where Adam remained physically alive after disobedience while fear, hiding and expulsion disclosed a changed relationship.

We should not simply insert Paul’s terminology into every detail of Genesis. The later passages nevertheless show that Scripture can speak of death where biological life continues. Adam’s eventual return to dust was not the only consequence requiring an answer.

Revelation presents another dimension:

“And death and hell were cast into the lake of fire. This is the second death.” Revelation 20:14

Here, death-language belongs to final judgment. Physical death, present alienation and the second death are distinguishable realities; they should not be treated as interchangeable expressions.

Nor does the existence of these different uses establish that every occurrence of death carries all three meanings equally. Each passage must be heard within its own argument.

In Romans 6, Paul contrasts the end of service to sin with eternal life in Christ. That contrast directs our attention beyond the biological cessation of life to the final outcome of sin’s dominion.

The wider biblical account illuminates the seriousness of that outcome. Sin breaks fellowship with God, humanity lives beneath mortality, and judgment lies beyond the grave. The Gospel must address the whole condition, not merely extend the years spent within it. The gift must answer the whole tragedy disclosed by the wages.

A further difficulty remains. Are people subject to death only because of their own individual acts, or does Paul describe a condition into which they enter before their personal moral history unfolds?

His argument takes us back to Adam.

Adam’s Act and Humanity’s Inheritance

Paul has traced sin’s entrance through one man and death’s spread throughout humanity. He then writes:

“Nevertheless death reigned from Adam to Moses, even over them that had not sinned after the similitude of Adam’s transgression, who is the figure of him that was to come.” Romans 5:14

Death reigned even where wrongdoing did not take the form of Adam’s transgression. Subsequent generations did not stand before the same tree under the same command.

Why, then, should his act concern people who were not there?

Paul does not ask us to pretend that every descendant personally took Adam’s fruit. He presents Adam’s act as having consequences for the humanity that followed him.

Ordinary experience offers a limited comparison. A person may inherit an estate affected by obligations created before his birth. He did not create those obligations, but they shape what he receives.

Similarly, a child enters a nation whose institutions and circumstances bear the consequences of earlier decisions. The child did not make those decisions, yet begins life within the reality they helped produce.

Such comparisons do not explain every aspect of Adamic inheritance. Sin is more than an estate’s liability, and humanity is not an institution we choose to join. They illustrate the narrower point that a condition can precede the person who enters it.

Christian traditions have described Adam’s relationship to his descendants differently. Some emphasise representative headship and the imputation of guilt; others give greater emphasis to inherited corruption and mortality. Those differences should be acknowledged without obscuring the common finding that humanity does not begin afresh from Adam’s original innocence.

Every generation enters a human order in which sin and death are already present. Our own conduct then confirms that the rebellion continues:

“For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God.” Romans 3:23

Adam’s descendants repeatedly seek life on terms other than God’s. The fallen condition provides no excuse for those choices; it is also expressed through them.

Scripture continues to uphold personal responsibility. Deuteronomy 24:16 forbids executing children for their fathers’ crimes, while Ezekiel 18:20 rejects the claim that a righteous son bears his father’s personal iniquity.

These passages resist the indiscriminate transfer of one person’s wrongdoing to another. Paul’s account of Adam concerns a distinct relationship: the consequences of the first man’s act for the humanity of which he stood at the beginning.

That relationship cannot be reduced to ordinary parenthood. Neither should its consequences be used to erase the responsibility of later generations for their own conduct.

We inherit a condition we did not originate and become accountable for the sins we commit within it. Recognising both facts prevents us from confusing the history of humanity with the moral record of an individual.

It also prevents mortality from becoming a crude measurement of personal wrongdoing. Infants die, people with diminished moral capacity die, and faithful believers die. The presence of a grave does not establish that a particular offence caused that death as an immediate punishment.

Mortality points to a shared condition, not a scale by which we can rank the deceased. Our judgments about particular wrongdoing require evidence beyond the fact that someone died.

Adam explains sin’s entrance into the human story. Our conduct confirms that it remains.

What the Wages Reveal

Death is more than a final payment attached to separate acts of misconduct. Its reign belongs to the human condition Paul describes through Adam, while Romans 6 exposes the outcome of continuing service to sin.

This does not make everyone equally wicked. The devoted parent and the violent offender do not bear identical records. Justice requires attention to conduct, intention and consequence.

Paul’s conclusion concerns the ground upon which humanity can stand before God:

“As it is written, There is none righteous, no, not one.” Romans 3:10

Relative goodness does not provide the sinless righteousness needed to establish an independent claim to acceptance. Isaiah’s confession supplies another searching expression of human inadequacy:

“But we are all as an unclean thing, and all our righteousnesses are as filthy rags…” Isaiah 64:6

The confession does not make every human act equally evil. It exposes the inadequacy of sinful people’s righteousness before the God whose mercy they need.

Scripture can recognise genuine integrity. Noah is described as just, Job as perfect and upright, and Zacharias and Elisabeth as righteous before God. Such descriptions acknowledge faithfulness without presenting their subjects as independent sources of sinless righteousness.

Human beings naturally compare themselves with one another. A person may be more generous than his neighbour, more honest than his colleague or less corrupt than a public offender. These differences matter.

They do not establish freedom from sin’s dominion or supply the power to overcome mortality. The person who swims farther than another still cannot cross an ocean by his own strength.

What the grave reveals, Genesis explains historically and Romans interprets doctrinally. Humanity lives within a condition in which sin and death reign together.

Our best achievements occur within that condition. They cannot, by themselves, deliver us from it.

Humanity Cannot Rescue Itself

Once the problem is understood, the reach of merely human remedies becomes clearer.

Education can address ignorance, institutional reform improve government and economic development relieve deprivation. Moral instruction can guide conduct, medicine treat disease and just laws restrain wrongdoing.

Each endeavour has genuine value. The question is whether any can accomplish the reconciliation and deliverance Paul’s diagnosis requires.

My professional life has taught me to respect what institutions can do. Law determines rights, imposes obligations and provides remedies when duties are breached.

Its judgments nevertheless have limits. A court may acquit a man of the charge before it; it cannot release him from mortality. A favourable verdict concerning one allegation does not settle his relationship with God.

Human progress becomes a false ground of confidence when we ask it to supply what lies beyond its capacity. Its value need not be diminished to recognise that boundary.

Even God’s Law reveals a distinction between stating righteousness and producing it within those commanded to obey. Paul writes:

“Therefore by the deeds of the law there shall no flesh be justified in his sight: for by the law is the knowledge of sin.” Romans 3:20

The defect was not in the Law. It disclosed God’s righteous standard and exposed humanity’s failure to meet it.

A mirror reveals a blemish without removing it. Similarly, the Law identifies wrongdoing but does not regenerate the person whose wrongdoing it reveals.

This places obedience within its proper relationship to salvation. Human effort can restrain harm and improve our common life, but it cannot establish that guilt has been answered before God or confer the life humanity lacks.

A person cannot restore fellowship with God simply by deciding that past rebellion no longer matters. Nor can accumulated achievement reverse the mortal condition shared with every generation.

If the wages of sin are death, humanity needs more than improved performance within sin’s dominion. The remedy must come from the God against whom it has rebelled.

The Sentence Turns

Romans 6:23 would leave humanity without hope if it ended with its first declaration. Sin has entered, death has followed and humanity cannot provide the life it needs.

Then the sentence turns.

The word “but” introduces a provision arising from another source. Paul does not announce a more favourable wage for people whose religious achievements outweigh their failures.

He calls it “the gift of God.”

That description excludes boasting: the recipient cannot claim to have earned what God freely gives. It also answers despair, because receiving the gift does not depend upon humanity first creating the life it lacks.

Sin pays its wages. God gives what those wages cannot provide.

Paul then identifies the One through whom the gift comes: “…through Jesus Christ our Lord.”

Those words determine the direction of the investigation. The remedy cannot be understood apart from the Person in whom God supplies it.

Part I has completed the diagnosis. Human experience presented mortality, Genesis traced its connection with rebellion, and Paul explained the relationship between Adam, sin’s dominion and death.

We have also distinguished the inherited condition from personal conduct, and bodily death from the wider judgment associated with sin. The problem reaches further than the grave alone, and no human achievement supplies its complete answer.

Paul’s sentence now turns us towards God’s provision. How did He prepare, accomplish and offer a gift that answers sin, judgment and death?

Part II follows that unfolding purpose.

The wages belong to sin. The gift belongs to God.

sections.html:
“And I will put enmity between thee and the woman, and between thy seed and her seed; it shall bruise thy head, and thou shalt bruise his heel.” Genesis 3:15

Paul’s sentence turns from the wages of sin to God’s gift, and locates it “through Jesus Christ our Lord.” How did God prepare humanity to recognise the One through whom that gift would come?

Before Adam and Eve were expelled from Eden, God addressed the serpent with words of conflict, injury and the bruising of its head. Though their full significance was not immediately apparent, Scripture’s unfolding testimony points towards a victory yet to be accomplished.

What began as an early indication of hope gradually took shape through divine promises and covenants, the Law and its sacrifices, Israel’s history and the prophetic witness. Each arose within its own historical context, while contributing to the unfolding purpose that would find its fulfilment in Christ.

But what did these promises mean for those who trusted God before Calvary, when the redemption towards which they pointed had not yet been accomplished?

The enquiry then reaches the Incarnation. Why was it necessary for the eternal Son to enter the very humanity He came to redeem? And how could He become truly human without sharing in humanity’s sin?

These questions lead us towards the Cross, where an even deeper mystery awaits: if death is the wages of sin, why would the One who knew no sin willingly submit Himself to it?

Part II traces the unfolding of God’s redemptive purpose from its earliest promise to its revelation in Jesus Christ, examining who He is and the life He lived before turning to the significance of the death He willingly embraced.

sections.title: The Promise Before Its Fulfilment
sections.html:
The Purpose Begins to Unfold

The biblical account of God’s answer to death did not begin in Bethlehem. It began in Eden.

Humanity had rebelled, fellowship with God had been broken and death pronounced as its consequence. Before Adam and Eve left the Garden, however, God spoke words that went further than the judgment upon them:

“And I will put enmity between thee and the woman, and between thy seed and her seed; it shall bruise thy head, and thou shalt bruise his heel.” Genesis 3:15

The words concern conflict between the serpent and the woman, and between their seed. There would be hostility and suffering. The serpent would wound, but the woman’s seed would strike his head. Read within Scripture’s unfolding testimony, they also point towards the overcoming of the deceiver.

The promise does not say how that victory will come, but it places hope within the judgment: the serpent’s apparent triumph will not be final.

Violence spread, wickedness increased and nations arose. God’s purpose became more visible when He called Abraham:

“Now the LORD had said unto Abram, Get thee out of thy country, and from thy kindred, and from thy father’s house, unto a land that I will shew thee: And I will make of thee a great nation… and in thee shall all families of the earth be blessed.” Genesis 12:1–3

God promised to make a nation from Abraham, but the blessing would extend to “all families of the earth.”

From Abraham came Isaac, from Isaac came Jacob and from Jacob came the tribes of Israel. Within that people, God preserved the promises through which His blessing would reach the nations.

Their calling did not rest on any natural superiority over others. The account points to God’s choice and faithfulness, and to the purpose for which He had appointed them.

Abraham himself stood before God by faith:

“Abraham believed God, and it was counted unto him for righteousness.” Romans 4:3

What, then, of Abraham and others who trusted God long before Bethlehem and Calvary?

They responded to what God had revealed, although its complete fulfilment remained ahead. Hebrews describes the faithful as having “died in faith, not having received the promises, but having seen them afar off” (Hebrews 11:13).

Their faith did not require every detail later revealed concerning Christ. Abraham trusted the God who had spoken; Christians look back upon the saving work that fulfilled His purpose.

Salvation has one foundation, whatever the difference in revelation. Paul describes Christ as the One:

“Whom God hath set forth to be a propitiation through faith in his blood, to declare his righteousness for the remission of sins that are past, through the forbearance of God.” Romans 3:25

Paul connects God’s earlier forbearance with Christ’s work. His patience towards past sins was not indifference; Christ’s redemption would demonstrate the righteousness of the God who had shown mercy before Calvary.

Hebrews makes the connection explicit. Christ is the Mediator of the new covenant:

“…by means of death, for the redemption of the transgressions that were under the first testament…” Hebrews 9:15

Christ’s death therefore provides the redemptive answer even for transgressions committed under the earlier covenant. Those who trusted God before Calvary did not receive salvation through a separate or independent means.

The promise came before its fulfilment, but Christ’s saving work remains the foundation of redemption across every generation.

A People Delivered and Instructed

Abraham’s descendants entered Egypt, multiplied and were subjected to oppression. Their circumstances might have suggested that God’s promises had been forgotten.

Scripture presents a different picture:

“And God heard their groaning, and God remembered his covenant with Abraham, with Isaac, and with Jacob.” Exodus 2:24

God had neither forgotten His people nor abandoned His promise. His remembrance signalled not a recovery of forgotten obligations, but His continuing faithfulness to the covenant He had established.

He raised Moses, confronted Pharaoh and delivered Israel from bondage. The Exodus became central to Israel’s remembrance of the God who had seen its affliction and acted.

On the night before their departure, judgment was coming upon Egypt. Israel was instructed to kill a lamb and place its blood upon the doorposts:

“And when I see the blood, I will pass over you.” Exodus 12:13

The blood had no power independent of God’s promise. Protection belonged to the provision He appointed, and the households were called to respond to His word.

Passover joined protection with departure. Those spared were to eat in readiness to leave, and the event would be remembered through a continuing observance in which children learned what God had done.

Families departed together as a people whom God would instruct in shared covenant life. Deliverance carried them towards a new allegiance and responsibilities under their Deliverer.

The significance of Passover becomes clearer in the New Testament, where Paul identifies its fulfilment in Christ: “For even Christ our passover is sacrificed for us.” 1 Corinthians 5:7

Paul makes this connection while addressing the moral life of the Corinthian church. As Israel’s deliverance called for a distinct way of life, so does Christ’s sacrifice. Those who belong to Him are to put away the sin and corruption inconsistent with their new life.

Deliverance from Egypt did not resolve Israel’s predicament. Those who witnessed God’s mighty acts repeatedly doubted and disobeyed Him. Freedom from Pharaoh’s oppression had not freed them from the rebellion within their own hearts.

The Exodus demonstrated God’s power to rescue His people. Their subsequent conduct exposed the need for a transformation within them.

At Sinai, God gave Israel His Law, revealing His holiness and establishing the standards by which His covenant people were to live.

The Law itself was holy, just and good, reflecting the righteousness of the God who gave it. The difficulty lay in the sinful condition of those called to obey, whose hearts remained resistant to the very righteousness it revealed.

Legal practice offers a comparison. A law can prescribe duties, identify prohibited conduct and attach consequences to a breach. Its existence alone does not remove the inclination to do what it forbids.

A statute may demand honesty without making those subject to it honest. Likewise, commandments inscribed upon stone could set the standard of obedience; they could not transform the hearts of those called to obey.

Paul writes:

“Therefore by the deeds of the law there shall no flesh be justified in his sight: for by the law is the knowledge of sin.” Romans 3:20

The Law exposed sin, revealing the gulf between God’s righteous standard and humanity’s failure to meet it.

Its role in God’s redemptive purpose was indispensable. Through it, Israel came to understand the demands of righteousness while exposing the inability to attain justification through obedience alone.

It could establish the standard, but not transform the heart. What humanity needed was more than instruction; it needed the inward renewal that only God could provide.

The Altar and the Cost of Sin

God did not give the Law and leave His people without an appointed means of approaching Him. Within their covenant life, He established sacrifice, priesthood and the altar:

“For the life of the flesh is in the blood: and I have given it to you upon the altar to make an atonement for your souls.” Leviticus 17:11

The initiative belonged to God. Those who violated His commands could not dismiss their wrongdoing or decide for themselves how atonement should be made.

Israel’s sacrificial system addressed different aspects of covenant life. Some offerings concerned specific offences; others dealt with impurity, thanksgiving or fellowship. Confession, priestly ministry and sacrifice each served their appointed purposes within the worship God established.

Through these provisions, Israel learnt that approaching a holy God required more than human sincerity. Cleansing and acceptable worship depended upon the means He prescribed.

The sacrifices fulfilled their covenantal purpose, providing atonement and cleansing as God ordained. They did not complete redemption. Offerings continued daily, at appointed festivals and across generations. Worshippers returned, and priests repeated their ministry.

That repetition raises a question. If these sacrifices had provided a complete and final answer to sin, why was another offering always necessary?

Hebrews describes the Law as:

“A shadow of good things to come, and not the very image of the things.” Hebrews 10:1

A shadow points beyond itself. Israel’s sacrifices served a real purpose within God’s covenant, while anticipating a fulfilment they could not themselves accomplish.

An animal’s death provided the atonement God prescribed, yet it could not transform the worshipper’s heart or end sin’s dominion.

The Law revealed God’s righteous standard; the altar provided an appointed means of approach for those who fell short of it. Together, they exposed humanity’s responsibility and its continuing dependence upon divine provision.

Even so, Israel’s people, priests and kings repeatedly failed. Greater resolve and stricter observance could not accomplish the inward renewal that was needed.

The question is larger than forgiveness for particular offences. What could deal with sin itself and transform the hearts of those held under its power?

When the Prophets Looked Ahead

The prophets spoke directly to the failures of their generation, confronting injustice, idolatry and religious observance that concealed persistent disobedience.

Their message was uncompromising. Sacrifice could not excuse rebellion, worship could not legitimise oppression, and ceremony could never replace faithfulness to God.

Prophetic testimony did not end with condemnation. Amid Israel’s repeated failures, the prophets proclaimed a divine purpose that looked past existing arrangements, pointing towards a remedy for the condition those failures had revealed.

Isaiah described a Servant whose suffering made the question of atonement personal:

“But he was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities: the chastisement of our peace was upon him; and with his stripes we are healed.” Isaiah 53:5

The wounds belong to the Servant; the transgressions belong to others. His suffering brings peace to people whose wrongdoing created their need.

Isaiah continues:

“All we like sheep have gone astray; we have turned every one to his own way; and the LORD hath laid on him the iniquity of us all.” Isaiah 53:6

Each has turned towards his own way, yet the iniquity is laid upon another.

The altar had taught Israel that sin required atonement. The prophet now spoke of a Person bearing the sins of others. How His suffering could answer their guilt remained a question for the fulfilment ahead.

Jeremiah confronted the related difficulty of obedience. Israel knew God’s commands but had repeatedly broken His covenant. Clearer instruction was not enough. What was needed was God’s transforming work within their hearts.

God promised:

“Behold, the days come, saith the LORD, that I will make a new covenant with the house of Israel, and with the house of Judah.” Jeremiah 31:31

The promised renewal included an inward relationship to His Law:

“I will put my law in their inward parts, and write it in their hearts.” Jeremiah 31:33

What had been placed before the people would take hold within them. The promise also addressed the wrongdoing that stood against restored fellowship:

“For I will forgive their iniquity, and I will remember their sin no more.” Jeremiah 31:34

Neither prophet traced the full manner of fulfilment. Together their promises brought the central need into focus: sin required atonement, and those reconciled to God needed inward renewal.

God had promised to address both. How would He bring these promises to fulfilment?

History Waiting for a Person

Eden, Abraham, Passover, Sinai, the altar and the prophets each belong to distinct moments in biblical history. Their significance must first be understood within the circumstances in which God revealed His purpose.

Viewed together, however, they show a progression. Eden introduced the promise of victory over the serpent; Abraham received the promise of blessing extending to the nations. Israel’s deliverance, the giving of the Law and the sacrificial system revealed God’s faithfulness and humanity’s need.

The prophets carried that expectation further, speaking of a Servant who would bear sin and a new covenant characterised by forgiveness and inward renewal. The promised answer was becoming more recognisable.

Each served its appointed purpose within a larger account whose fulfilment still lay ahead.

But who could accomplish what the sacrifices could not finally secure? Through whom would the promised blessing reach the nations?

The New Testament finds the answer in a Person, Jesus Christ.

In the fullness of time, the eternal Son entered the human history that had awaited His coming.

sections.title: And God Became Man
sections.html:
When God Entered His Own World

The Old Testament closes with a promise still awaiting fulfilment.

Abraham trusted God without witnessing its completion. Moses served within its unfolding purpose, David celebrated it in song, and the prophets described it with increasing clarity. Generations passed, but fulfilment remained dependent upon God’s faithfulness.

Then God entered the world He had created.

Israel awaited its promised Redeemer, though expectations differed concerning His identity and mission. Some longed for a king who would overthrow foreign oppression; others anticipated a prophet like Moses or the restoration of David’s kingdom.

God’s answer came as a child, born in a manger in Bethlehem. To understand who that child was, John takes us back past Bethlehem and Israel’s history to the beginning of all things:

“In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.” John 1:1

Before describing what Jesus did, John establishes His identity. The One who entered history already existed, and all things were made through Him.

Bethlehem was the beginning of the Son’s human life, not of His existence.

John then declares:

“And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us.” John 1:14

The eternal Word became truly human without ceasing to be God. The One through whom all things were created entered the world He had made.

It was the Son who became incarnate, not the Father or the Holy Spirit. He did not surrender His deity or assume humanity as a temporary appearance. The eternal Son took to Himself a complete human nature.

Nothing humanity had accomplished obliged Him to come. We had not earned His mercy, and we had found no means of restoring the fellowship our rebellion had broken.

God Himself came to us.

What had been anticipated through generations of promise and prophecy now entered human history in the Person of Jesus Christ.

Why Humanity Was Necessary

Why did the eternal Son become man?

God had sent prophets, given His Law and delivered His people from oppression. Israel’s history nevertheless showed a need that instruction and earthly deliverance could not resolve.

Sin had entered human life, fellowship with God had been broken and death had followed. Redemption had to reach the people living within that condition.

Hebrews says: “Forasmuch then as the children are partakers of flesh and blood, he also himself likewise took part of the same.” Hebrews 2:14

Those He came to redeem were people of flesh and blood. He shared their humanity, entering the life He had come to restore.

Jesus was conceived and born, grew within a family and occupied a definite place in history. His body was real, and so was the human life expressed through it.

Complete humanity includes more than a body. Jesus possessed a human mind, affections and will. Luke records that He “increased in wisdom and stature” (Luke 2:52), while the Gospels describe His sorrow, compassion and prayer.

His human mind was not replaced by divine knowledge, and His human willing was real. In Gethsemane, His words “not my will, but thine, be done” (Luke 22:42) show His human response to the suffering before Him.
