The early Christian theologian Gregory of Nazianzus defended the completeness of Christ’s humanity in his first letter to Cledonius, commonly designated Epistle 101. Opposing the claim that Christ lacked a human mind, he insisted that what was not assumed could not be healed.

His argument was fundamental to the doctrine of redemption: if human nature was to be restored, the Son had to assume it in its fullness, including the human mind.

Jesus did not need to experience every occupation, marriage or old age to be fully human. He shared the fullness of human nature, not every possible human experience.

There are not two persons in Christ. The eternal Son Himself lived a truly human life, and everything He experienced, bodily and inwardly, belonged to the one divine Person who had become man.

Sin is not an essential attribute of human nature. Adam was fully human before his rebellion. Sin entered through disobedience and corrupted humanity without becoming part of what makes us human.

The eternal Son could therefore assume a complete human nature without assuming its sinful corruption. He shared our true humanity, including its capacity for suffering and death, but remained entirely without sin.

God’s answer reached human life from within: the Word became flesh.

Why God Was Necessary

Human history had known prophets, priests, kings and reformers. Some served God faithfully, but none could redeem humanity from a condition to which he himself remained subject.

Even the finest moral example can inspire righteous living. It cannot secure divine forgiveness, reconcile humanity to God or overcome the dominion of death.

John’s declaration is therefore decisive:

“The Word was God.” John 1:1

The One who assumed our humanity was Himself the Creator, possessing the divine authority and power necessary to accomplish what fallen humanity could never achieve.

Human beings could acknowledge their guilt, repent and seek mercy. But forgiveness belonged to the God against whom they had sinned. They could not absolve themselves or set aside the consequences of their rebellion by their own authority.

In an ordinary dispute, the wrongdoer cannot resolve the matter simply by declaring the offence forgiven. Such a declaration does not answer the injured party’s claim or repair the harm caused.

The distinction is one of authority: those responsible for a wrong cannot unilaterally determine its resolution. Reconciliation with God must therefore proceed from His own initiative and provision.

The eternal Son supplied the provision by entering the humanity He came to redeem. The One through whom human life was created had Himself undertaken the work of its restoration.

In On the Incarnation, particularly sections 7–8, Athanasius connects creation and restoration. The Word through whom humanity was made was able to renew His work when it had become subject to corruption.

Humanity required more than a messenger proclaiming the need for restoration. The Creator Himself had entered history to accomplish its redemption.

Paul declares:

“For in him dwelleth all the fulness of the Godhead bodily.” Colossians 2:9

The fullness dwells in Him bodily. His human nature does not diminish His deity, and His deity does not make His humanity a pretence.

The Church developed language to safeguard both truths: Jesus Christ is one Person, the eternal Son, fully God and fully man, possessing two complete and distinct natures united without confusion or division.

He is not a mixture of deity and humanity, and His identity is not divided between them. The eternal Son who existed with the Father before creation is the One who was born into human history and lived among us.

The One who truly shares our humanity is also the eternal God, with the authority and power to accomplish what humanity could never secure for itself.

In the Fullness of Time

If God had spoken in Eden, why did centuries pass before the Son came?

Abraham died before the fulfilment, Moses gave the Law, and the prophets announced what lay ahead. Yet God had not forgotten His word.

Paul writes:

“But when the fulness of the time was come, God sent forth his Son, made of a woman, made under the law.” Galatians 4:4

The verse has three parts. God sent forth his Son: His coming proceeded from the Father’s initiative. Made of a woman: His entrance involved real human birth. Made under the law: He entered Israel’s covenant history and obligations.

Christ came within the purpose already unfolding through promise, covenant, sacrifice and prophecy. His arrival was not an improvised response to an unexpected crisis.

Historical circumstances also helped the Gospel spread. Israel had preserved the Scriptures, widely understood languages aided communication, and roads connected territories across the Roman Empire.

Such circumstances help explain the setting of the apostolic mission, though not why God appointed that moment for His Son’s coming.

Paul points to God’s action. The initiative and timing belonged to the One who had governed His purpose from the beginning.

The centuries of preparation had taught His people to recognise their need. The Law stated righteousness, sacrifice gave guilt an appointed response, and prophecy announced forgiveness and renewal.

God did not need that history to discover the answer. Through it, He prepared His people to understand the answer He would give.

When the appointed time came, the eternal Son entered that history Himself.

The God Who Walked Among Men

The wonder of the Incarnation lies in who came and in the life He lived among us.

The Son grew within a family, worked, travelled and experienced hunger and weariness. He entered homes, attended a wedding, welcomed children and wept beside a friend’s grave.

These encounters matter because they show the reality of His human life. He did not merely pass through humanity while remaining untouched by its ordinary experiences.

John says that the Word “dwelt among us” (John 1:14). The expression recalls God’s presence with His people in the tabernacle. In the incarnate Son, that presence was encountered on village roads, beside the sea and around household tables.

His greatness did not make those encounters less personal. The conversations, meals and tears belonged to the human life He had fully assumed.

Paul describes His coming:

“Who, being in the form of God, thought it not robbery to be equal with God: But made himself of no reputation, and took upon him the form of a servant, and was made in the likeness of men.” Philippians 2:6–7

The Son’s humility consisted in taking the servant’s condition without relinquishing His divine identity. He willingly accepted a life of dependence, service and suffering.

Human authority is often used to preserve distance and privilege. The One with the highest authority drew near, receiving the people whose need others avoided.

Bethlehem did not complete His mission. John the Baptist identified the purpose towards which His coming pointed:

“Behold the Lamb of God, which taketh away the sin of the world.” John 1:29

The title recalls the sacrificial provision traced in the preceding chapter. It points to what Christ would accomplish, but first to the life of the One named as the Lamb.

He had entered the world in which sin and death reigned. Had He, too, committed sin? Did death have a claim upon Him for wrongdoing of His own?

sections.title: The Enigma of Jesus Christ
sections.html:
The Obedient Man

The Incarnation establishes who Jesus Christ is: the eternal Son, truly God and truly man. His identity raises another question: what did the life He lived as man mean for humanity’s redemption?

If death entered the human story through Adam’s disobedience, what would it mean for another Man to confront the same demand for obedience and still remain faithful where Adam had failed?

The Gospels confront that question almost immediately:

“Then was Jesus led up of the Spirit into the wilderness to be tempted of the devil.” Matthew 4:1

Having just been publicly declared the beloved Son of the Father, Jesus is led into the wilderness. Before His public ministry unfolds, Scripture places Him before the adversary whose deception first appeared in Eden.

The first man stood in a garden surrounded by God’s provision. When temptation came, he distrusted God’s Word and chose another way.

Christ stood in a wilderness marked by hunger, solitude and physical weakness.

Satan appealed to hunger, identity and authority, all legitimate realities, but proposed that Jesus pursue them independently of the Father’s appointed will.

Beneath the individual temptations lay the question first encountered in Eden: would He trust the Father, or determine His own way?

Jesus refused the invitation. He would not abandon His dependence upon the Father or use His divine power at the tempter’s prompting to evade the trial before Him.

He responded in true human obedience, despite hunger and testing and grounding each answer in Scripture:

“It is written.” Matthew 4:4, 7, 10

Three times He answered the tempter with those words. Each answer showed more than resistance, but obedience and trust in the Father.

The Son who had entered the human condition would accomplish His mission in willing submission to the Father’s will, even when obedience brought great suffering.

Augustine later urged Christians to recognise that Christ’s temptation was real and was undergone for those He came to save. He met the tempter from within our condition.

Temptation is not itself sin, and real obedience does not mean the absence of testing. Jesus experienced the full reality of temptation without yielding to it.

Where the first Adam disobeyed amid abundance, Christ obeyed amid deprivation.

Perfectly Sinless

The victory in the wilderness was no isolated act of resistance. It revealed the obedience that would mark Jesus’ whole earthly life.

Scripture records the devotion of its most faithful servants without concealing their failures. Obedience and weakness sit within the same lives.

Noah found grace in the eyes of the LORD, yet later succumbed to drunkenness. Abraham trusted God’s promises but faltered in moments of fear. Moses faithfully led Israel out of Egypt, yet himself disobeyed God’s command. David, despite his devotion to God, fell into grievous sin, while Peter, who professed unwavering loyalty to Jesus, denied the very Lord he loved.

Their failures do not erase their faithfulness.

However exemplary their service, none could become humanity’s Saviour while remaining subject to the very condition from which humanity needed deliverance.

Jesus Christ stands in a different category. His opponents scrutinised His conduct, religious leaders tested His words and political authorities examined Him. The New Testament speaks of His character as it speaks of no one else’s.

Peter, who had observed Him closely, writes:

“Who did no sin, neither was guile found in his mouth.” 1 Peter 2:22

Paul describes Him as the One:

“Who knew no sin.” 2 Corinthians 5:21

Hebrews declares:

“For we have not an high priest which cannot be touched with the feeling of our infirmities; but was in all points tempted like as we are, yet without sin.” Hebrews 4:15

These declarations describe One in whom sin was absent.

His humanity remained real. He knew hunger, weariness, sorrow, opposition and pain.

We sometimes imagine that sinfulness makes us truly human. Scripture says the opposite: sin corrupts the humanity God created.

Christ’s sinlessness revealed human life ordered towards God as it was intended to be. His fidelity showed humanity without rebellion.

Every other morally accountable person requires mercy for personal sin. Jesus carried no guilt of His own as He came to rescue others from theirs.

The Righteousness Humanity Could Not Produce

The problem identified in Part I was deeper than occasional misconduct.

Sin had entered through Adam’s disobedience, and successive generations confirmed its presence through their conduct. The Law revealed what righteousness required, but fallen humanity could not render the complete obedience it demanded.

Christ brought a new fact into the argument: a truly human life lived in complete obedience to God.

Biblical righteousness demands more than the absence of wrongdoing. It includes wholehearted love for God, trust in His Word and obedience to His will.

A distinction familiar to legal practice helps clarify the point. An acquittal establishes that a particular charge has not been proved; it does not certify that the accused has fulfilled every obligation or lived an entirely righteous life.

Scripture makes a stronger claim concerning Jesus. His accusers could establish no wrongdoing, but His righteousness extended beyond the absence of guilt. The Gospels reveal a life of willing, complete obedience to the Father.

He declared:

“I do always those things that please him.” John 8:29

In Jesus, these words express the governing direction of His entire life. His obedience did not wait for moments of public scrutiny.

It governed the years before His ministry, His conduct among His disciples and His response when submission became costly. Jesus’ life between Bethlehem and Calvary formed part of His saving work.

Humanity had done what God forbade and withheld the obedience He required. Christ, by contrast, approached Calvary having fulfilled that obedience without fault or compromise.

He came righteous. Every temptation resisted, every command obeyed and every act of submission formed part of an unbroken life of faithfulness to the Father.

Within the world disordered by Adam’s rebellion, Jesus lived the human obedience Adam had failed to render.

The Last Adam

Paul places Christ directly alongside Adam:

“For as by one man’s disobedience many were made sinners, so by the obedience of one shall many be made righteous.” Romans 5:19

Paul sets two men at turning points in the human story. The first man’s disobedience brought condemnation; the obedience of Christ brings righteousness and life.

Paul makes the contrast again:

“For as in Adam all die, even so in Christ shall all be made alive.” 1 Corinthians 15:22

Adam and Christ stand at the head of different orders. Adam represents humanity under sin and death; Christ represents the new humanity whose life rests in Him.

Paul carries the comparison further:

“And so it is written, The first man Adam was made a living soul; the last Adam was made a quickening spirit.” 1 Corinthians 15:45

The title “the last Adam” identifies Christ as God’s final answer. His coming was no experiment to discover whether a later man might succeed where Adam failed.

The early Christian theologian Irenaeus understood Christ’s redemptive work in terms of recapitulation: the eternal Son entered humanity’s history, taking up what Adam had disordered and answering his disobedience through His own perfect obedience.

Christ entered a history marked by rebellion to restore the humanity whose relationship with God had been fractured by it.

Where Adam distrusted God, Christ remained faithful. Where Adam asserted independence, Christ submitted to the Father.

Paul writes:

“For if by one man’s offence death reigned by one; much more they which receive abundance of grace and of the gift of righteousness shall reign in life by one, Jesus Christ.” Romans 5:17

Paul builds the passage on contrasts: offence and obedience, condemnation and righteousness, death and life.

A moral example can demonstrate the demands of obedience. It cannot reverse humanity’s rebellion or break the dominion of death.

The last Adam came to accomplish what fallen humanity could never secure for itself.

The Life That Owed Death Nothing

That contrast returns to the verse on which this book rests:

“For the wages of sin is death.” Romans 6:23

Adam sinned and death entered. His descendants inherited mortality and continued the rebellion through sins of their own.

Before us now stands another Man. Jesus shared the world in which hunger, sorrow, friendship and rejection belong to ordinary life. He was tempted and suffered, but Scripture says He “did no sin” and “knew no sin.”

If death is sin’s wage, what wages had He earned?

None. His obedience was complete, and there was no personal wrongdoing for which death was due.

Christ’s human nature was capable of suffering and bodily death. He shared “flesh and blood” (Hebrews 2:14), and the Gospels testify that His death was physically real.

Capacity to die and guilt deserving judgment are different questions. Christ possessed a body capable of death without having committed the sin that could make death His earned wage.

Every ordinary human life unfolds within the condition introduced through Adam. Christ entered that world as the sinless Son.

He nevertheless prepared to give Himself to death.

That is the enigma of Jesus Christ.

Why Did Jesus Die?

Our enquiry began by asking why humanity dies.

Jesus changes the question. Why did the sinless Man die?

Historical explanations identify the events leading to His execution. Religious authorities accused Him, Rome possessed the power to crucify and Pontius Pilate authorised the sentence.

The physical mechanism explains how His life ended. The political and religious circumstances explain how He came to be condemned. Neither explains why He knowingly moved towards that death.

His death was no unforeseen end to a mission He had expected to survive. Jesus travelled towards Jerusalem, spoke of what awaited Him and prepared His disciples.

He declared: “I lay down my life, that I might take it again. No man taketh it from me, but I lay it down of myself.” John 10:17–18

His words do not excuse those who betrayed, condemned or crucified Him. Their hostility did not reduce Him to a helpless victim of events He could not foresee or resist.

He freely laid down His life.

The theological question is larger than the injustice of killing an innocent person. Human history contains many such tragedies, and innocence alone does not explain Christ’s deliberate movement towards Calvary.

According to Scripture’s account, the eternal Son had entered our humanity and lived in complete obedience. He then knowingly accepted death.

His own sin cannot explain it, and the circumstances of an execution cannot exhaust the purpose He announced.

Why did the Man who owed death nothing willingly die?

sections.title: Part III
sections.subtitle: Redemption Accomplished
sections.html:
“…but now once in the end of the world hath he appeared to put away sin by the sacrifice of himself.” Hebrews 9:26

Hebrews presents Christ’s death not merely as the suffering of an innocent Man, but as a sacrifice directed towards the removal of sin. His innocence and willing submission now direct our attention beyond the fact of His death to its redemptive significance.

How could the Sinless One bear the judgment of sins He had not committed, and how could God forgive the guilty without setting aside His justice? What did Jesus complete when He declared, “It is finished”?

Beyond the Cross, the enquiry turns to the empty tomb. Why was death unable to hold Christ, and what distinguishes His Resurrection from those previously restored to mortal life? What does His victory establish concerning the completeness of His redemptive work and the power of death?

These questions bring us back to the promise with which our investigation began. If Christ’s death and Resurrection confront the dominion of sin and death, what becomes possible for those He came to redeem?

Paul directs us to the other half of his declaration:

“…but the gift of God is eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord.” Romans 6:23

What is the nature of eternal life, and why is Christ its only source? How can it be received as God’s gift without being reduced to a reward for human merit or religious effort?

Part III moves from Christ’s identity and obedient life to the accomplishment of redemption: the Cross, the Resurrection and the gift secured through Him.

sections.title: The Irony of the Cross
sections.html:
Justice Satisfied

At Calvary, the connection between sin and death confronts us with an innocent Man.

Jesus Christ had lived without sin, fulfilling every demand of righteousness through perfect obedience to the Father. Why, then, did He voluntarily surrender His life upon a Roman cross?

Here lies the irony. The innocent stood in the place of the condemned. The One who held divine authority submitted to human judgment, and what appeared to be the defeat of God’s Son was the means by which God accomplished His redemptive purpose.

The answer begins with God’s character. He is holy and righteous, loving and gracious. His mercy does not disregard His righteousness; both belong to who He is.

Humanity’s predicament is more serious than moral imperfection. Sin is rebellion against the Creator, and the God who offers forgiveness cannot treat that rebellion as though it were unreal.

Consider a judge who knew an offence had been committed but declared it unimportant simply to appear compassionate. We would question what had happened to justice.

God is not a human judge, and the Cross cannot be reduced to a courtroom procedure. Yet the comparison presses the question: how can He forgive the guilty without making light of the wrong?

No rule of justice stands above God, and His righteousness is no external restraint upon His love. He acts consistently with His own holy nature, in which justice and mercy do not compete.

The Psalmist expresses this harmony:

“Mercy and truth are met together; righteousness and peace have kissed each other.” Psalm 85:10

Spoken within a prayer for Israel’s restoration, these words picture mercy and righteousness as partners in God’s dealings with His people.

Chapter Four traced Israel’s preparation through sacrifice, priesthood and prophecy. Isaiah made atonement personal:

“Surely he hath borne our griefs, and carried our sorrows… he was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities: the chastisement of our peace was upon him; and with his stripes we are healed.” Isaiah 53:4–5

The wounds are the Servant’s; the transgressions belong to others. Isaiah describes suffering through which peace comes to those who could not provide it for themselves.

He continues:

“All we like sheep have gone astray; we have turned every one to his own way; and the LORD hath laid on him the iniquity of us all.” Isaiah 53:6

The people wander, while the Servant bears their iniquity. His suffering demands an explanation beyond personal wrongdoing.

At Calvary, Judas betrayed Jesus, religious leaders demanded His condemnation, Pilate authorised His execution and Roman soldiers carried it out. Scripture does not excuse their actions.

Their wrongdoing did not defeat God’s redemptive purpose. The Cross was not an accident requiring a later remedy, and God was not a detached spectator of cruelty.

The Son had willingly embraced the path that led to Calvary. Yet His suffering on behalf of others raises a question of justice, and Scripture itself asks it.

The Innocent Bearing the Guilty

Scripture insists that people are answerable for their own wrongdoing:

“The son shall not bear the iniquity of the father.” Ezekiel 18:20

The Law likewise commands:

“Every man shall be put to death for his own sin.” Deuteronomy 24:16

Proverbs states the principle bluntly:

“He that justifieth the wicked, and he that condemneth the just, even they both are abomination to the LORD.” Proverbs 17:15

How, then, can the Cross be called just? Does saying that Jesus suffered for the guilty amount to praising the condemnation of the One who did not deserve it?

The objection cannot be dismissed by appealing vaguely to mystery. Saying that God punished an unrelated innocent person would leave the difficulty intact.

Jesus’ willingness matters, but consent alone does not resolve it. An innocent stranger could volunteer to serve a criminal’s sentence; that would not make the judgment lawful or just.

What the men who condemned Jesus did and what God purposed through the Cross are different acts. Their verdict treated Him as an offender; Scripture identifies Him as the righteous Son giving Himself for offenders. Calling His sacrifice just does not vindicate the betrayal, false accusation or abuse of authority through which He suffered.

The same event can display human injustice and divine provision. God’s purpose did not turn the perpetrators’ wrongdoing into obedience; it brought salvation through the self-giving of the One against whom they acted.

The New Testament gives four answers.

First, His death was voluntary: “No man taketh it from me, but I lay it down of myself.” John 10:18

Those who betrayed and executed Him remained responsible. They did not compel an unwilling Son; He fulfilled the redemptive purpose He shared with the Father.

Second, He was not unrelated to those He came to save. Paul places Him opposite Adam as the representative of a new humanity:

“For as by one man’s disobedience many were made sinners, so by the obedience of one shall many be made righteous.” Romans 5:19

He did not appoint Himself, and humanity did not choose Him by agreement. God sent His Son to enter our condition and stand as the righteous Head of those He came to redeem.

That does not make Jesus personally guilty of their acts. His obedience, within God’s appointed purpose, carries consequences for those He represents.

Third, the One who gave Himself was the incarnate Son. God did not require a separate innocent party to bear a cost from which He remained removed. In Christ, He entered human life and supplied the provision His righteousness required.

John Stott emphasised this in The Cross of Christ. Substitution must be understood through the Son’s willing self-giving within God’s one saving purpose, rather than as punishment imposed upon an unwilling third party.

Fourth, Scripture expressly says that Christ bore the sins of others:

“Who his own self bare our sins in his own body on the tree.” 1 Peter 2:24

Peter does not stop at Christ’s courage under unjust treatment, still less at any wrongdoing of His own. He says that Christ bore our sins.

The Son gives Himself freely, stands as God’s appointed Representative, supplies God’s own provision and bears the sins of those He came to save. Calvary is not an ordinary criminal proceeding with a substituted defendant. Human legal comparisons raise the objection but cannot explain the incarnate Son’s unique act.

Paul describes God as: "…just, and the justifier of him which believeth in Jesus.” Romans 3:26

God does not declare guilt harmless in order to forgive. He provides in Christ the righteous ground upon which the guilty are justified.

The Great Exchange

Paul gives a further account:

“For he hath made him to be sin for us, who knew no sin; that we might be made the righteousness of God in him.” 2 Corinthians 5:21

Christ’s sinlessness remains explicit within the statement. The One made “to be sin for us” had no personal guilt requiring judgment.

Jesus did not become sinful or corrupt, and He never ceased to be the Father’s beloved Son.

Some understand the expression to carry the sense of a sin offering; others emphasise His representative bearing of guilt. In either reading, Paul distinguishes the One who knew no sin from those for whom He acted.

Our wrongdoing did not become something Christ personally committed. Nor does receiving His righteousness permit us to claim His obedient life as our own achievement. He willingly bore the judgment our sin required.

The exchange preserves the distinction between guilt and obedience. God knows the guilt is ours and the obedience Christ’s.

The distinction between bearing sin and committing sin is no qualification added to protect Christ’s reputation. It belongs to the meaning of His sacrifice. Had He been answering for His own wrongdoing, His death would not present the contrast Paul describes.

The offering is the righteous One Himself, acting for those whose guilt is real. God does not mistake the guilty for innocent people. His acceptance of them rests upon Christ’s provision, while His knowledge of their history remains true. Mercy answers their guilt without requiring a false account of their lives.

The Man who had earned no wage of death entered it for others, while those with no righteousness of their own find their hope in Him.

His work also answers the relationship broken by sin. The Cross provides the ground of reconciliation between guilty humanity and the holy God against whom it rebelled. How that reconciliation becomes the possession of particular people comes later.

Love and Mercy Revealed

Justice and substitution explain essential aspects of the Cross. God’s love reveals why He acted for the guilty.

Paul writes:

“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.” Romans 5:8

His action did not await humanity’s becoming worthy. Christ died for people still in rebellion against God.

John writes:

“Herein is love, not that we loved God, but that he loved us, and sent his Son to be the propitiation for our sins.” 1 John 4:10

We misunderstand this love if we imagine the Father desired judgment while the Son desired mercy. Scripture presents one saving purpose: the Father sends in love, and the Son gives Himself willingly.

The Father and the Son remain distinct persons, yet there is no conflict between them. Propitiation does not mean humanity supplied an offering to persuade an indifferent God to care.

John begins with God’s love because the provision proceeds from Him. The sacrifice expresses His mercy; it does not create it.

Propitiation means that Christ’s sacrifice deals with sin and satisfies God’s righteous wrath against it. God Himself provides the answer; He does not forgive by treating evil as inconsequential.

The word carries both holiness and mercy. The God against whom humanity has sinned supplies the answer in His Son, at a cost humanity could never bear for itself.

His love does not persuade His righteousness to look away. In love, He acts righteously to save, taking human guilt seriously while opening the way to forgiveness.

The New Testament also describes Christ’s work through sacrifice, ransom, reconciliation and victory. These complementary descriptions show different aspects of the same saving act.

Sacrifice concerns His offering of Himself. Ransom speaks of liberation at great cost, reconciliation of restored fellowship, and victory of the defeat of the powers holding humanity in bondage.

Justice and substitution receive most attention here because this enquiry concerns death as sin’s wage. No one image exhausts the Cross.

At Calvary, God confronted humanity’s rebellion and bore the cost of saving those who had turned against Him.

It Is Finished

As Jesus hung upon the Cross, had the offering anticipated through Israel’s sacrifices been completely made?

John records:

“When Jesus therefore had received the vinegar, he said, It is finished: and he bowed his head, and gave up the ghost.” John 19:30

His words announce the completion of the work entrusted to Him.

Israel’s priests repeatedly returned to the altar. Their sacrifices served appointed purposes without bringing redemption to its final accomplishment. Christ offered Himself once.

The Cross and the Resurrection are distinct events. His offering was completed at Calvary; His rising would show that death could not hold Him.

There is no unfinished portion of atonement for humanity to supply. Moral effort, religious observance and personal sacrifice cannot make His offering more complete. No practice Christ gives His Church supplies a deficiency in His once-for-all offering.

Christ’s completed offering does not erase every consequence of sin. Forgiveness does not make past wrongdoing harmless or remove the suffering it caused. Completeness belongs to the offering, not to the disappearance of sin’s effects.

This is why the Cross can be proclaimed with both gratitude and seriousness. The cost has been borne by Christ, rather than dismissed as unimportant or transferred back to those He came to redeem.

The irony has reached its sharpest point. The innocent has given Himself for the guilty, and an instrument of condemnation has become the place of God’s saving provision.

To those watching, His death appeared to settle the matter against Him. His disciples scattered, His accusers seemed vindicated and a stone would close His tomb.

His offering was complete. But if death held the sinless Son, how could His work bring the promised victory?

The answer would come on the first day of the week.

sections.title: Death Could Not Hold Him
sections.html:
The Empty Tomb

The events of Calvary ended with the body of Jesus laid inside the tomb of Joseph of Arimathaea.

Jesus had truly died. Roman soldiers witnessed His final moments, His side was pierced and Joseph, together with Nicodemus, prepared His body for burial.

The stone sealed the tomb of One who had willingly entered death after completing His sacrifice. He was no wounded man awaiting recovery or rescue.

For the disciples, that burial appeared to bring everything to a bewildering end. The One they had followed and confessed as Messiah now lay behind a stone.

Instead of waiting expectantly for victory, they withdrew in fear and sorrow. They could not reconcile His death with the promises they had heard from His own lips.

The women who came to the tomb on the first day of the week show how final the burial seemed. They did not come awaiting a risen Lord; they came carrying spices for a dead body.

Their devotion remained steadfast. Their expectations followed the ordinary course of human experience: the dead remained in their graves.

Luke records what they found:

“And they found the stone rolled away from the sepulchre. And they entered in, and found not the body of the Lord Jesus.” Luke 24:2–3

The empty tomb confronted them with a reality for which grief had left them unprepared. Their first response was perplexity, not rejoicing.

The body was gone, but an empty grave did not explain itself.

Before confusion could give way to understanding, heaven supplied the explanation:

“Why seek ye the living among the dead? He is not here, but is risen.” Luke 24:5–6

These words mark a turning point in human history. The tomb stood empty, but Jesus had not avoided death, and no one had removed His body. He had truly died, entered the grave and risen beyond its dominion.

The Resurrection was more than a welcome conclusion to His earthly ministry. It was the act of God by which the obedient Son was raised, vindicated and revealed as Lord.

The empty tomb became the first historical sign that Calvary had not ended in defeat. The appearances of the risen Christ would supply the confirming explanation.

The disciples did not arrive at this conviction through immediate religious enthusiasm. The Gospel accounts repeatedly describe fear, uncertainty and disbelief before understanding emerged.

The apostles attributed their certainty to encounters with the risen Christ. Paul later placed the Christian faith squarely upon the Resurrection:

“And if Christ be not risen, then is our preaching vain, and your faith is also vain.” 1 Corinthians 15:14

Paul leaves no room for ambiguity. Christianity rests not merely upon the wisdom of Christ’s teaching, the perfection of His example or even the wonder of His sacrificial death. Its foundation is the proclamation that the One who died was raised from the dead.

If Christ did not rise, the apostolic Gospel loses its foundation. If He did, the Cross stands revealed not as the tragic end of a righteous Man, but as the accomplished sacrifice of the Redeemer over whom death could claim no lasting victory.

Why could death not hold Him?

Beyond Death’s Dominion

Peter addressed that question on the Day of Pentecost:

“Whom God hath raised up, having loosed the pains of death: because it was not possible that he should be holden of it.” Acts 2:24

Peter declares more than death’s failure to hold Jesus. He insists that it was impossible for Christ to remain under its dominion.

The impossibility did not arise from some independent law operating above God, and the Resurrection was not an automatic result of Christ’s sinlessness. God raised His Son in fulfilment of His purpose and promise.

Peter immediately grounds his declaration in David’s prophetic words::

“Neither wilt thou suffer thine Holy One to see corruption.” Acts 2:27

David had died, been buried and undergone corruption. Peter therefore argued that the words of the Psalm looked beyond David to the promised Christ.

The Holy One would enter death, but He would not be abandoned to it’s power. God’s promise, His redemptive purpose and the identity of His Son assured that the grave could never become His final resting place.

Death entered through sin and established its dominion over Adam’s descendants. Jesus Christ entered the same realm without personal sin.

He did not die because His own guilt demanded judgement. He willingly surrendered His life in obedience to the Father, accomplishing the sacrifice through which human guilt would be answered.

Jesus had declared before Calvary:

“No man taketh it from me, but I lay it down of myself. I have power to lay it down, and I have power to take it again. This commandment have I received of my Father.” John 10:18

His life was not wrested from Him as though Calvary had overtaken Him against His will. Even in death, He remained the obedient Son.

The Resurrection was therefore not an unexpected correction of Calvary, but the vindication of the Son who had perfectly fulfilled the Father’s will. He truly entered death, but God did not leave His Holy One beneath its power.

From Adam onwards, death had reigned over successive generations. At the Resurrection, that dominion was decisively broken.

Paul states the contrast plainly:

“For since by man came death, by man came also the resurrection of the dead.” 1 Corinthians 15:21

Scripture records instances of the dead being restored to life long before Easter. Through the ministries of Elijah and Elisha, the dead were raised; Jesus Himself restored Jairus’s daughter, the widow’s son and Lazarus to life.

These events do not diminish the uniqueness of Christ’s Resurrection. They were restorations to mortal existence, not deliverance from mortality itself. Those raised resumed lives still subject to death and would eventually face the grave again.

Christ rose differently:

“Christ being raised from the dead dieth no more; death hath no more dominion over him.” Romans 6:9

He did not return to resume the mortal life that had ended at Calvary. He rose into incorruptible life, beyond death’s dominion.

Paul therefore calls Him:

“The firstfruits of them that slept.” 1 Corinthians 15:20

Christ is the firstfruits, not because no one had previously returned from death, but because His Resurrection inaugurated a life over which death would never again exercise dominion.

Athanasius recognised this distinction. Christ’s Resurrection was not simply the restoration to mortal existence; in the risen body of the Son, the power of corruption had been overcome.

The One who emerged from the tomb was the very Jesus who had been crucified, now risen beyond the reach of death, never to die again.

Many Infallible Proofs

The Resurrection was not left as a private event known only to heaven.

Christ did not ascend immediately after rising. He remained with His disciples for forty days, establishing that the One who had been crucified was alive.

Luke records:

“To whom also he shewed himself alive after his passion by many infallible proofs, being seen of them forty days, and speaking of the things pertaining to the kingdom of God.” Acts 1:3

The apostolic proclamation rested on more than the discovery of an empty tomb. Those commissioned to proclaim the Resurrection testified to repeated encounters with the risen Christ.

Jesus walked with two disciples on the road to Emmaus, explaining the Scriptures concerning Himself. He appeared among the apostles behind closed doors, invited Thomas to examine His wounds and shared a meal with His disciples beside the Sea of Galilee.

The Gospels present the risen Christ neither as a memory preserved by grief nor as an idea fashioned by His followers. They testify to encounters with the very Lord who had been crucified, now alive and recognised by those who had known Him before Calvary.

His risen life possessed bodily reality. He could be seen, heard and touched, and He ate in the presence of His disciples. He was no longer subject to the mortality from which He had risen. Continuity and transformation met in the same risen Lord.

N. T. Wright has emphasised that resurrection, within the Jewish hope embraced and transformed by the earliest Christians, did not mean merely that a person’s soul survived death or that his influence continued. It concerned the restoration and transformation of embodied life beyond death.

The apostles therefore did not proclaim the survival of Christ’s spirit or the continuing power of His teaching. They proclaimed that the Crucified One had risen bodily from the grave.

Paul preserved an early summary of that proclamation:

“Christ died for our sins according to the scriptures; And that he was buried, and that he rose again the third day according to the scriptures.” 1 Corinthians 15:3–4

Paul then lists appearances to Cephas, the Twelve, more than five hundred people at once, James, all the apostles and finally himself. Of the larger group, Paul adds:

“Of whom the greater part remain unto this present.” 1 Corinthians 15:6

The claim was not presented as a secret revelation. It was proclaimed publicly while several named witnesses and many of the five hundred were still alive.

Testimony must still be carefully examined, and doesn’t warrant unquestioned acceptance. It does establish that belief in the Resurrection arose early and publicly, on the assertion that numerous witnesses had encountered the risen Christ.

The transformation of the disciples strengthens that testimony. Before the Resurrection, they were fearful and uncertain. Peter denied Jesus and the others fled.

Within weeks, these same followers publicly proclaimed His Resurrection in Jerusalem, despite mounting opposition, imprisonment and the threat of death.

Their willingness to suffer does not, by itself, prove that their conclusions were correct. People may sincerely suffer for beliefs that are false. It does, however, weigh strongly against the suggestion that the disciples knowingly invented encounters they knew had never occurred.

Their explanation remained straightforward: they had seen the risen Christ.

Peter therefore declared:

“This Jesus hath God raised up, whereof we all are witnesses.” Acts 2:32

Christianity rests on historical claims. The Gospel calls us to trust the God who entered human history, died and, according to apostolic testimony, rose again.

The forty days also prepared the disciples for His departure and for the mission that would follow.

Risen and Exalted

If Jesus Christ had triumphed over the grave, what followed?

Luke records:

“And when he had spoken these things, while they beheld, he was taken up; and a cloud received him out of their sight.” Acts 1:9

The Ascension was no disappearance of One whose earthly mission had ended. It marked the visible departure of the risen Christ, and it revealed that the Crucified One had been exalted to heavenly glory and authority.

The cloud carries particular significance. Throughout Scripture, the cloud frequently marks manifestations of God’s presence and glory.

Jesus was not simply moving from one place in the physical universe to another. He was being received beyond the disciples’ sight into the glory of the Father’s presence where He reigns with divine authority.

Paul describes His exaltation:

“Wherefore God also hath highly exalted him, and given him a name which is above every name.” Philippians 2:9

The movement begun earlier in Paul’s declaration now reaches its conclusion. The One who humbled Himself, took the form of a servant and became obedient unto death is highly exalted.

The writer to the Hebrews connects that exaltation directly with the completed sacrifice of Calvary:

“But this man, after he had offered one sacrifice for sins for ever, sat down on the right hand of God.” Hebrews 10:12

The old covenant’s priests continued to minister because sacrifices continued to be offered. Christ offered “one sacrifice for sins for ever” and sat at the Father’s right hand. His seated position does not suggest inactivity; it signifies the completeness of His offering and the authority of His reign.

The Ascension belongs to the same redemptive movement as the Cross and Resurrection.

The Cross completed Christ’s sacrificial offering. The Resurrection revealed that death could not hold Him. The Ascension displayed the risen Son exalted at the Father’s right hand.

The One who had been mocked as King now reigns.

From the Empty Tomb to the Gift

The wages of sin had brought our enquiry from Eden to the grave. The Resurrection has now established that death did not have the final word over Jesus Christ.

Paul’s declaration goes further, to the gift towards which the Cross and Resurrection point:

“…but the gift of God is eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord.” Romans 6:23

We have followed the meaning of the wages and examined the work of the Redeemer. The enquiry now turns to the gift His redemption has made possible.

sections.title: The Gift of Eternal Life
sections.html:
Wages and Gift Revisited

Paul’s sentence has two halves. The first is the verdict:

“For the wages of sin is death.” Romans 6:23

A wage is earned. Paul uses that language because death is the due consequence of sin. But his sentence does not end there. It names a gift.

Paul does not offer eternal life as a better wage to those who obey more successfully or accumulate sufficient religious merit. He calls it a gift.

A gift does not become due because the recipient has established a right to it. It proceeds from the giver’s generosity. Everything we have examined about sin and death has excluded the possibility that humanity could claim eternal life as an entitlement.

Paul tells us whose gift it is and where it is found. God gives eternal life “through Jesus Christ our Lord.” The gift cannot be separated from the Son through whom God provides it.

Christ has accomplished the saving work. Humanity did not perform it and cannot improve upon it.

Eternal life is free to its recipients because Christ has borne the cost of providing it. The first question is what it is.

What Is Eternal Life?

Eternal life can sound like another name for existence that never ends. Duration is certainly part of the promise: the life God gives does not expire at the grave.

But would endless existence, by itself, answer everything that went wrong in Eden? Humanity’s loss concerned more than the number of years it could live. Fellowship with God was broken.

Jesus described eternal life in relational terms:

“And this is life eternal, that they might know thee the only true God, and Jesus Christ, whom thou hast sent.” John 17:3

To know God here is more than to possess accurate information about Him. It is to be brought into fellowship with the One from whom sin had alienated humanity.

Eternal life answers a deeper loss than mortality alone. It is life reconciled to God through His Son. Its duration matters, and so does the relationship that gives it its character.

John tells us where that life is found:

“And this is the record, that God hath given to us eternal life, and this life is in his Son. He that hath the Son hath life.” 1 John 5:11–12

Eternal life cannot be possessed independently of Christ. John declares that this life “is in his Son.” To receive it is to belong to the risen Lord.

This also explains why Scripture speaks of eternal life as both present and future. The believer may know God through Christ now, while still awaiting the removal of death and the resurrection of the body.

The gift begins now and runs past the grave, because its source is the One whom the grave could not hold.

Through Jesus Christ Alone

Why does Paul say that eternal life comes “through Jesus Christ our Lord”? Why could God’s gift not simply be detached from Him?

The answer lies in the condition from which humanity needed rescue and in what Christ alone accomplished. Sin had broken fellowship with God. Another lesson about right conduct could not, by itself, restore that fellowship or remove the judgment sin had brought.

The Son became human, lived without sin, gave Himself at the Cross and rose beyond death’s dominion. No other teacher, prophet or reformer could claim that work.

Jesus said:

“I am the way, the truth, and the life: no man cometh unto the Father, but by me.” John 14:6

That is an exclusive claim, and readers are right to take it seriously. Its basis is not a preference for one religious figure over others. It is the Christian claim about who He is and what He has done.

If Jesus Christ became human, bore sin and rose from death, His work cannot be treated as a remedy available elsewhere. The question is whether this account is true. If so, reconciliation is inseparable from Him.

After the Resurrection, Peter declared:

“Neither is there salvation in any other: for there is none other name under heaven given among men, whereby we must be saved.” Acts 4:12

Peter was not offering his hearers a choice among competing methods of self-improvement. He was announcing the Saviour whom God had given.

Paul likewise writes:

“For there is one God, and one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus.” 1 Timothy 2:5

A mediator must be able to stand in relation to those being reconciled. Christ is truly human, sharing the nature of those He came to save. He is also the eternal Son, able to provide what no fallen human being could supply.

The gift is found in Him because God provided the Mediator who accomplished our reconciliation, rather than leaving humanity to find its own way back.

Eternal life is found in the Son alone. The question, then, is how those separated from God by sin can enter into fellowship with Christ and share in the life He gives.

The Gift Bestowed

The work of Christ did not become inactive when He ascended into heaven. Before His Ascension, He told His disciples:

“But ye shall receive power, after that the Holy Ghost is come upon you: and ye shall be witnesses unto me both in Jerusalem, and in all Judaea, and in Samaria, and unto the uttermost part of the earth.” Acts 1:8

The Old Testament records the Spirit empowering people for particular tasks. Its prophets also looked towards a fuller work of God among His people.

At Pentecost, Peter explained what the gathered crowd had seen and heard:

“Therefore being by the right hand of God exalted, and having received of the Father the promise of the Holy Ghost, he hath shed forth this, which ye now see and hear.” Acts 2:33

Peter connected the Spirit’s outpouring directly to the exalted Christ. Pentecost was not a new saving project beginning after the Cross. The crucified and risen Son had been exalted, and He poured out the promised Spirit.

Jesus had said of the Spirit:

“He shall glorify me: for he shall receive of mine, and shall shew it unto you.” John 16:14

The Spirit does not direct believers away from Christ or begin a rival work. He bears witness to the Son and brings believers into living fellowship with Him.

The Father sent the Son. The Son accomplished the work entrusted to Him. The Holy Spirit brings people into the life secured by the risen Christ. The Persons act distinctly within the one redemptive purpose of God.

The apostles therefore preached more than a set of moral teachings left behind by a departed founder. They bore witness to a living Saviour who continued His work through the Spirit He had sent.

Eternal life is more than a possibility awaiting the believer at death. How, then, does a person receive the gift?

The Faith That Receives

After all we have considered about sin, judgment and the cost of redemption, the answer may seem almost too simple: salvation is received by grace through faith.

Human instinct expects a costly gift to require a costly payment from its recipient. We may assume that God must be waiting for enough obedience, devotion or religious achievement to make His gift deserved.

But that would turn the gift back into wages. Christ has accomplished the saving work. The sinner is called to trust Him, not to complete what He left unfinished.

Paul writes: “For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: Not of works, lest any man should boast.” Ephesians 2:8–9

Grace identifies the source of salvation. Christ’s completed work is its foundation. Faith receives what God provides.

Augustine insisted, particularly in On Grace and Free Will, that grace is not a reward for merit humanity has already established. God’s gracious initiative comes first.

Does that mean conduct no longer matters?

Paul immediately continues: “For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus unto good works.” Ephesians 2:10

The works excluded as the ground of salvation appear as the fruit of a life God has begun to change. They have a place, but it is not the place occupied by Christ’s work.

James examines the same question from the other side:

“Even so faith, if it hath not works, is dead, being alone.” James 2:17

Saying we trust someone and actually trusting them are not always the same thing. James asks whether a professed faith that disregards Christ’s words is alive. Works are not a second price for salvation; they reveal whether the profession has substance.

The order matters: grace gives, faith receives and the life received begins to bear fruit.

Faith must not become a disguised achievement. What matters is the Christ we trust, not how strong we feel.

In legal practice, a party’s confidence does not give a valid judgment its authority. The judgment rests upon the court’s lawful decision; the party relies upon what has been established.

Faith does not improve Christ’s sacrifice or make His Resurrection more effective. It rests upon Him. It is often described as an empty hand receiving a gift, although the gift received is inseparable from the Person who gives life.

The New Testament also calls hearers to repent, confess Christ and receive baptism. Peter called his hearers to repent and be baptised (Acts 2:38), while Paul spoke of believing in the heart and confessing Jesus as Lord (Romans 10:9).

These are not competing prices for salvation. They describe a response to the Gospel in which a person turns from sin and false grounds of confidence, trusts Christ, acknowledges Him as Lord and receives baptism in obedience to His command.

Repentance is a turning from the ways in which we have resisted Him. Faith rests upon the Saviour to whom we turn.

Life That Begins Now

Jesus declared:

“For God so loved the world, that he gave his only begotten Son, that whosoever believeth in him should not perish, but have everlasting life.” John 3:16

The verse begins with God’s love and gift. Human belief responds to what He has provided in His Son. John later writes:

“He that believeth on the Son hath everlasting life.” John 3:36

John says “hath.” The believer does not merely wait for eternal life to begin after the grave. Through Christ, fellowship with God has begun already.

The gift excludes pride and despair. No one can claim to have earned it or make personal performance the foundation of hope.

Paul’s sentence can now be read whole:

“For the wages of sin is death; but the gift of God is eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord.” Romans 6:23

But one difficulty remains. People who possess eternal life still become ill, suffer loss, grow old and die. What does Christ’s victory mean for life now, and when will death finally be gone?

That is the enquiry of the final Part.

sections.title: Part IV
sections.subtitle: Living in the Victory of Christ
sections.html:
“Nay, in all these things we are more than conquerors through him that loved us.” Romans 8:37

Paul’s declaration concerns believers living amid suffering, loss and danger. Their confidence rests upon Christ’s love in the midst of them. What does His victory mean for people who possess eternal life but remain mortal?

The final Part follows the gift into the believer’s life.

Why do Christians ordinarily continue to die, and what does resurrection hope say to those who grieve? What confidence does the believer have beyond the grave?

The Holy Spirit forms the life received through Christ. What should grace produce in personal conduct, relationships and the shared life of the Church? How can assurance sustain repentance and not breed complacency?

Then Christ returns, and death is finally destroyed. What will that day mean for those who have died and those who remain alive? Scripture’s promise runs from bodily resurrection to a renewed creation and God’s presence with His people.

The gift already received gives direction to life now; its promised fullness grounds the believer’s hope.

sections.title: Why Christians Still Die
sections.html:
Defeated, But Still Present

Few questions arise more naturally from the Gospel than this: if Jesus Christ has conquered sin, defeated death and bestowed eternal life upon His people, why do Christians still die?

The question is not theoretical. Every generation of believers has buried fathers and mothers, husbands and wives, sons and daughters. Christian cemeteries stand beside Christian churches. Funeral hymns are sung by those who confess that Christ has risen from the dead.

The apparent contradiction is impossible to ignore.

The answer lies in Christ’s victory and the present stage of redemption. The New Testament teaches that He has decisively defeated death, though it remains within the present order until its final destruction.

Paul writes that Jesus Christ:

“Hath abolished death, and hath brought life and immortality to light through the gospel.” 2 Timothy 1:10

The same Apostle looks towards the future and declares:

“The last enemy that shall be destroyed is death.” 1 Corinthians 15:26

The two statements agree. Through His death and Resurrection, Christ has broken death’s final dominion and brought life and immortality into the open. Death nevertheless remains part of present human experience. It is still an enemy whose decisive defeat has already occurred but whose complete removal still lies ahead.

Christ has already entered death and risen beyond its dominion. The graves of His people still await emptying, and their mortal bodies still await transformation.

In Christ and Time, Oscar Cullmann likened this to the difference between a decisive battle and the final end of a war. Once the determining battle has been won, the outcome is settled even though conflict continues until the final surrender.

The Resurrection is the decisive battle; death’s final destruction is certain because that battle is already won.

The same pattern marks Christian life. Sin has been judged, though believers still struggle with it. Satan has been decisively defeated but continues to oppose God’s people until his final destruction.

Christ reigns at the Father’s right hand, while Scripture still looks towards the day when every enemy will be visibly placed beneath His feet.

Romans 8 gives the clearest answer. Paul begins with the believer’s changed standing before God:

“There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus.” Romans 8:1

For those who belong to Christ, physical death is no longer the payment by which personal guilt must be answered. Christ has borne condemnation, and the believer does not enter the grave to complete what His sacrifice left unfinished.

Paul nevertheless acknowledges the continuing mortality of the body:

“And if Christ be in you, the body is dead because of sin; but the Spirit is life because of righteousness.” Romans 8:10

The believer has life in Christ while still inhabiting a body subject to death. Eternal life has begun, but bodily immortality remains a promise awaiting manifestation.

Paul therefore describes Christians as waiting for:

“The adoption, to wit, the redemption of our body.” Romans 8:23

The believer is reconciled to God and shares Christ’s life, but the mortal body still awaits redemption. Physical death remains possible until that promised transformation.

The circumstances of a believer’s death remain within God’s providence. For those in Christ, death is not condemnation and cannot become their final condition.

Christians still die because their mortal bodies await the full manifestation of Christ’s victory. His conquest of death has not failed.

Not All Shall Sleep

Physical death remains the ordinary experience of believers, but the New Testament does not teach that every Christian must undergo it.

Paul reveals what he calls a mystery:

“Behold, I shew you a mystery; We shall not all sleep, but we shall all be changed.” 1 Corinthians 15:51

All shall be changed. Not all shall sleep. Paul develops the same truth when describing the return of Christ:

“Then we which are alive and remain shall be caught up together with them in the clouds, to meet the Lord in the air.” 1 Thessalonians 4:17

Believers alive at Christ’s return will therefore be transformed without first passing through ordinary bodily death. Their mortal condition will not continue unchanged; the same divine purpose that raises believers who have died will transform those who remain alive.

Enoch and Elijah, met in Chapter One, show that God is sovereign over each person’s experience of death. Christ’s victory goes deeper: it answers the sin underlying death’s reign.

Christ came to deal with sin itself, reconcile humanity to God and break the dominion death had exercised since Adam.

The transformation of believers alive at His return will form part of the complete manifestation of that victory.

Grief Without Despair

The victory of Christ does not require Christians to pretend that death has ceased to be painful.

When Lazarus died, Jesus knew that resurrection was moments away. The grave before Him would shortly surrender the man it held.

Even so, Scripture records its shortest verse:

“Jesus wept.” John 11:35

Those tears were not the tears of uncertainty. Jesus stood before the grave as the Lord of life, fully aware that He would soon call Lazarus forth, and He entered the sorrow death had produced.

Why would the One who was about to raise Lazarus weep? Because death remained what it had been since Eden: an enemy.

Resurrection hope does not ask us to call death good because Christ has conquered it. Jesus shared the sorrow of those who mourned.

Christian hope therefore does not suppress grief. Paul writes:

“But I would not have you to be ignorant, brethren, concerning them which are asleep, that ye sorrow not, even as others which have no hope.” 1 Thessalonians 4:13

Paul does not say that Christians do not sorrow. He says that they do not sorrow as those who have no hope.

A Christian funeral remains a funeral. Separation is painful, absence is real and tears require no apology.

What faith changes is the conclusion. For those who belong to Christ, the grave is no longer evidence that death has finally prevailed. The believer belongs to the One who entered the grave and rose again.

Tears and hope walk together until faith gives way to sight.

Beyond the Grave

If physical death is no longer condemnation, what confidence does the Christian have beyond it?

Scripture answers by directing believers to Christ. Christian hope rests upon the historical reality that Jesus Christ died, rose again and now lives at the Father’s right hand.

Paul speaks plainly as he faces his own mortality:

“For to me to live is Christ, and to die is gain.” Philippians 1:21

Those words overturn the assumptions by which humanity ordinarily measures life and death.

Outside Christ, death appears to take away everything that gives earthly life meaning. For Paul, however, death could not take away his greatest treasure because that treasure was Christ Himself.

Life remained precious. It gave him opportunity to serve Christ and strengthen others. Death could nevertheless be called gain, because it could not separate him from the Lord he loved.

Paul explains:

“Having a desire to depart, and to be with Christ; which is far better.” Philippians 1:23

His confidence is personal. He does not long for relief from suffering or escape from the burdens of earthly life. He desires to be with Christ.

Humanity’s tragedy began with alienation from God in Eden. The believer’s hope beyond death is therefore unhindered fellowship with the risen Lord who has reconciled him to God.

Death does not sever the believer’s relationship with Christ. When earthly life ends, the believer remains with the Lord to whom he already belongs.

Presence with Christ after death is not complete redemption. God created humanity as embodied persons. His final purpose is not to preserve souls apart from their bodies while graves still bear witness to death’s work.

Scripture therefore looks past the believer’s presence with Christ to the redemption of the body. That greater hope belongs to a later chapter.

For now this is enough: death does not separate the believer from Christ.

Death Without Defeat

Christians still die because the eternal life they have in Christ has not fully transformed their mortal bodies. Reconciled to God and freed from condemnation, they await the bodily redemption His victory has secured.

Physical death therefore remains within the present order and ordinarily within Christian experience. It is still an enemy, still a source of grief and still a consequence of the Fall. For those in Christ it is no longer condemnation.

Death cannot add to Christ’s completed sacrifice, overturn His salvation or sever believers from Him. It may end their earthly lives, but cannot determine their eternal destiny.

Christian confidence rests in the One who has mastered death. The believer faces mortality with realism. He does not call death good, and he does not forget that Christ has risen. He grieves its separations and trusts the Lord into whose presence he will enter when earthly life ends.

The Christian lives between two certainties: the victory Christ has already accomplished and the consummation God has promised.

This interval is the life in which faith is tested, character is formed, love is practised and the risen Christ is made known through those who belong to Him.

The Gospel changes how Christians die. It also changes how they live before death comes.

sections.title: The Life The Gift Produces
sections.html:
The Spirit Within

The gift of eternal life, once received, begins at once to change the believer.

Peter declared on the Day of Pentecost:

“Repent, and be baptized every one of you in the name of Jesus Christ for the remission of sins, and ye shall receive the gift of the Holy Ghost.” Acts 2:38

Paul speaks of believers hearing and trusting the Gospel:

“In whom ye also trusted, after that ye heard the word of truth, the gospel of your salvation: in whom also after that ye believed, ye were sealed with that holy Spirit of promise.” Ephesians 1:13

The Holy Spirit is God’s personal presence within His people. God does not forgive them and then leave them to produce the Christian life by their own strength.

Paul writes:

“But ye are not in the flesh, but in the Spirit, if so be that the Spirit of God dwell in you.” Romans 8:9

Weakness and temptation remain, but a decisive change has occurred. The believer’s life now includes the indwelling of God’s Spirit.

John Calvin described the Holy Spirit as the bond by which believers are united to Christ. The description helps us understand why eternal life cannot be held independently of the Son. Through the Spirit, believers share the life found in Him.

This union concerns more than adopting Christ’s teaching as a personal philosophy. The risen Lord is the One upon whom His people depend, and His Spirit works within them.

Jesus expressed that dependence through the image of a vine and its branches:

“I am the vine, ye are the branches: He that abideth in me, and I in him, the same bringeth forth much fruit: for without me ye can do nothing.” John 15:5

A branch does not become fruitful by deciding that it no longer needs the vine. Its growth depends upon the life it receives. Christian maturity likewise deepens dependence.

That dependence matters when old weaknesses resurface. One who resolved never to respond angrily may feel anger rising again; another may find that success has revived an old reliance on personal strength.

At such moments, prayer brings the need before God, Scripture exposes the excuse, and correction from another believer may help us recognise what we have avoided. Dependence means receiving that help and acting on it.

The Spirit awakens new desires, exposes sin and strengthens obedience. Paul describes the fruit:

“But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, longsuffering, gentleness, goodness, faith, Meekness, temperance…” Galatians 5:22–23

Fruit reveals the life from which it grows. These qualities do not purchase eternal life; they express its presence in those who belong to Christ.

A Life Being Transformed

Grace changes both the believer’s standing before God and the believer himself.

Justification concerns acceptance before God through Christ. Sanctification concerns the continuing work by which the Holy Spirit forms His character within us.

The ground of acceptance is complete. The person accepted continues to need instruction, correction and growth.

Paul describes that transformation:

“But we all, with open face beholding as in a glass the glory of the Lord, are changed into the same image from glory to glory, even as by the Spirit of the Lord.” 2 Corinthians 3:18

The language describes an ongoing work. Belonging to Christ does not make every habit disappear immediately, but it changes the direction in which a person is called to live.

Paul writes:

“For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus unto good works, which God hath before ordained that we should walk in them.” Ephesians 2:10

Good works have their appointed place within the life God creates. Grace excludes boasting without removing obedience.

The believer therefore has responsibilities:

“Work out your own salvation with fear and trembling.” Philippians 2:12

Paul immediately identifies the source of that willing and working:

“For it is God which worketh in you both to will and to do of his good pleasure.” Philippians 2:13

God’s work does not make the believer passive. It enables the response Paul commands.

God works within; the believer works out.

In his Confessions, Augustine prayed that God would grant what He commands and then command what He wills. Obedience itself depends upon grace.

That dependence does not permit us to wait indefinitely for obedience to become effortless. We may need to apologise while pride still resists, refuse temptation while its attraction remains or keep a commitment when enthusiasm has faded.

The Spirit’s work enters these choices. We learn to seek His help and obey, whether weakness tempts us to make excuses or to despair of change.

Growth may be uneven. Its reality appears in a new willingness to receive correction, resist familiar wrongdoing and return to Christ when we fail.

A Life Shared with Others

The life received from Christ places the believer among others who belong to Him. Paul writes:

“Now ye are the body of Christ, and members in particular.” 1 Corinthians 12:27

The image preserves both belonging and individuality. Each member matters, but none has every gift or can fulfil the whole body’s calling alone.

The Church is therefore where transformation meets other people. Patience must meet real inconvenience, gentleness must govern difficult conversations, and love must make room for people whose needs interrupt our preferences.

Consider a respected member whose manner repeatedly wounds others. When someone approaches him about it, he may initially regard correction as an insult to his standing or an intrusion upon his service.

Grace gives him reason to listen. He can ask what happened, acknowledge the words he used and apologise without making the injured person responsible for his anger. Acceptance in Christ frees him to admit wrong without defending an image of faultlessness.

The person offering correction has responsibilities too. Paul instructs:

“Brethren, if a man be overtaken in a fault, ye which are spiritual, restore such an one in the spirit of meekness; considering thyself, lest thou also be tempted.” Galatians 6:1

Restoration requires truth spoken with humility. Correction becomes another offence when it humiliates the person, spreads the matter unnecessarily or treats the corrector as immune from similar failure.

Paul continues: “Bear ye one another’s burdens, and so fulfil the law of Christ.” Galatians 6:2

A bereaved household may need more than comforting words. Members can prepare meals, arrange transport, attend to children or contribute towards necessary expenses. Care also means asking what is needed and respecting the family’s dignity.

Such help often continues after public attention has moved elsewhere. The member who returns weeks later to listen or complete an ordinary task may carry a burden that a crowded first visit could not reach.

Disappointment within the Church also tests the life we profess. Two members may have trusted one another over a responsibility, only for one to fail and the other to bear the cost.

Forgiveness does not require pretending that nothing happened. They may need a direct conversation, an apology, practical repair and clearer arrangements. Grace teaches them to seek restoration without confusing it with concealment or immediate trust.

Christian communities themselves require repentance. Customs can protect pride, influence can silence legitimate concerns, and apparent harmony can hide unresolved wrongs. The Church grows by attending to truth, including truth that exposes her own failures.

Paul describes the body’s growth through “speaking the truth in love” and “that which every joint supplieth” (Ephesians 4:15–16). Christ forms His people through their faithful contribution to one another’s lives.

No Condemnation, No Complacency

Continuing failure can create deep uncertainty. If eternal life has been given, why does the believer still struggle?

Paul speaks into that anxiety:

“There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus, who walk not after the flesh, but after the Spirit.” Romans 8:1

The declaration concerns those who are “in Christ Jesus.” Walking after the Spirit describes their new direction; it does not supply a payment by which acceptance is purchased.

Paul announces a present reality grounded in Christ’s work. Its judicial meaning gives substance to its comfort.

Legal practice recognises the importance of finality. A concluded judgment cannot be reopened merely because a party dislikes its result. This illustrates confidence resting upon an established ground.

A human verdict does not explain every aspect of salvation, and a past profession of faith does not make a person’s present relationship with Christ irrelevant.

For those who belong to Jesus, failure does not make His completed sacrifice insufficient. Repentance returns them to the Saviour upon whom their acceptance rests.

Sin grieves the Father, disrupts fellowship and requires confession. The believer’s wrongdoing must be addressed within the relationship established through Christ.

The Spirit exposes sin with restoration in view. His conviction removes excuses and directs us towards confession, repentance and renewed dependence.

Despair takes a different course. It persuades us that our guilt has placed us beyond mercy, even as Christ calls us to return, and it makes us afraid to come.

Assurance makes real repentance possible. Because acceptance rests upon Christ, the believer need not protect himself by denying what he has done.

Assurance is not presumption. The same chapter warns:

“For if ye live after the flesh, ye shall die: but if ye through the Spirit do mortify the deeds of the body, ye shall live.” Romans 8:13

A person who grieves over sin and seeks help to resist it responds differently from one who claims grace as permission to refuse Christ’s authority. The distinction concerns the relationship to sin, not the number of failures.

That difference is not always easy to judge. A distressed conscience may exaggerate every weakness, while a confident profession may conceal a refusal to repent.

Paul’s warning calls us to examine ourselves and depend upon the Spirit.

Continuing faith receives correction and returns to Christ after failure. Perseverance is lived through dependence.

The believer’s confidence rests upon Christ. Repentance, obedience and growth bear witness to His work and never replace it.

The Shape of the New Life

The Spirit turns the believer towards God. Where guilt once prompted hiding, reconciliation gives access.

Our Lord taught His disciples to pray:

“After this manner therefore pray ye: Our Father which art in heaven, Hallowed be thy name.” Matthew 6:9

Our Father expresses belonging; Hallowed be thy name preserves reverence. Nearness does not diminish the majesty of the One who welcomes us.

The believer prays because Christ has established the relationship. Prayer becomes the conversation of a child bringing gratitude, need, confession and uncertainty before the Father.

Paul explains that access: “For through him we both have access by one Spirit unto the Father.” Ephesians 2:18

Through the Son, by the Spirit, believers approach the Father. Some days bring ready words; others bring only the effort to pray. Access rests upon Christ rather than eloquence.

Hebrews therefore declares:

“Let us therefore come boldly unto the throne of grace, that we may obtain mercy, and find grace to help in time of need.” Hebrews 4:16

Boldness is confidence in the One through whom we come. It enables us to bring needs we might otherwise conceal.

Prayer also prepares us to act. The help sought before God may be needed in a conversation, a financial decision or a responsibility awaiting our attention.

Consider a professional who discovers an error likely to damage a client’s interests. Concealment may protect his reputation briefly, but it leaves another person exposed to harm.

Grace gives him reason to acknowledge the mistake, explain its consequences and seek a remedy. Confidence in Christ does not remove the cost; it frees him from treating reputation as something that must be preserved through dishonesty.

An employee may face a payment that requires a false entry, or an entrepreneur an advantage obtained by withholding what another person is owed. Refusing may mean losing money, approval or opportunity.

Such choices reveal whether gratitude is more than words. The believer seeks God’s help to do what is right even when the favourable outcome cannot be guaranteed.

The demand may be quieter at home. A parent promises time to a child, then finds unfinished work pressing for attention. Faithfulness may require putting the work aside and keeping the promised conversation.
