None of these acts makes God a debtor. They belong to the responsibilities entrusted to someone who has received His grace.

Failure in these settings also requires practical repentance. A confession should lead, where possible, to correcting the record, returning money, keeping the neglected promise or asking forgiveness from the person harmed.

As fellowship deepens, the believer discovers that grace’s greatest privilege is knowing God Himself. Forgiveness, reconciliation and eternal life awaken gratitude because they have been received through Christ.

Worship, prayer and service become responses to that generosity. They become bargaining when we use them to place God under obligation.

Religion can become transactional: we give to secure a larger return, obey to demand a preferred outcome or pray as though the right words compel an answer. The Gospel teaches us to receive God’s gifts without claiming authority over His decisions.

Paul writes:

“In every thing give thanks: for this is the will of God in Christ Jesus concerning you.” 1 Thessalonians 5:18

Thanksgiving does not require calling every experience good. It recognises God’s faithfulness amid circumstances whose meaning we may not understand.

The life of grace therefore includes petition and gratitude. We seek help, fulfil our responsibilities and entrust the outcome to the Father.

Growing in Grace

Christian character does not appear fully formed at the beginning. Peter exhorts:

“But grow in grace, and in the knowledge of our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ.” 2 Peter 3:18

Growth requires time, but time alone does not guarantee it. The believer is called to attend to the knowledge, practices and relationships through which God forms His people.

So it is with spiritual formation: waiting for positive results does not excuse neglect of prayer, Scripture, fellowship or responsibilities already understood.

We should not despise small beginnings. Someone once quick to retaliate may pause, listen and choose a gentler answer. Another may begin to confess a wrong previously defended.

Such changes may attract little public notice. Their significance lies in the altered response to God and neighbour.

Disappointment also tests growth. Does service continue without recognition? Is correction received? Can we rejoice in another’s success without resentment?

These questions turn attention from religious appearance to the character being formed. They should prompt prayer and self-examination, not comparison with someone whose struggles we cannot fully see.

Eternal life takes visible form in people who remain dependent upon Christ. The Christian life is measured less by how long we have known Him than by how His character is becoming evident in our conduct.

Perfection awaits the believer. Desires require correction, habits require discipline and failures require confession.

God nevertheless continues His work. By the Spirit, He teaches His people to live from acceptance, receive help from one another and grow in faithful responsibility.

The transformation is real, though its completion remains ahead. Eternal life has begun, and the Spirit is at work.

sections.title: O Death, Where Is Thy Sting?
sections.html:
Christ’s Promised Return

Sin entered the world through Adam, and death followed. From Eden onwards, the grave appeared to have the final word over every human life. Then God’s Son became human, lived without sin, bore sinners’ judgment and entered a death He did not owe. On the third day, He rose beyond its dominion.

But the Resurrection of Christ was not the final scene of redemption. The risen Lord ascended to the Father and promised that He would return.

On the night before His crucifixion, Jesus told His disciples:

“Let not your heart be troubled: ye believe in God, believe also in me. In my Father’s house are many mansions… I go to prepare a place for you. And if I go and prepare a place for you, I will come again, and receive you unto myself; that where I am, there ye may be also.” John 14:1–3

At the centre of the believer’s hope, Christ places His own coming. He does not promise only relief from suffering or entrance into a better world. “I will come again… that where I am, there ye may be also.”

From the moment sin drove humanity from the presence of God in Eden, redemption has moved towards the restoration of that broken fellowship. The covenants anticipated it and the sacrifices foreshadowed it. The Incarnation revealed it, the Cross secured it and the Resurrection guaranteed it.

Christ’s return will bring it to consummation. The Christian’s greatest hope is to dwell forever with Christ.

This is why the New Testament directs the believer’s attention to a Person, not to speculation about dates and timetables. Christ did not command His disciples to calculate the day of His return. He commanded them to remain faithful until He came.

In Mere Christianity, C. S. Lewis observed that the Christians who did most for the present world were often those who thought most seriously about the next. Expectation of Christ’s return does not diminish responsibility in this life; it gives that responsibility direction.

Because history belongs to Christ, believers may labour, endure and serve. Nothing done for Him is without eternal significance.

The Lord Himself Shall Descend

What, then, will Christ’s return mean for those who have already died in Him?

Paul answers:

“For the Lord himself shall descend from heaven with a shout, with the voice of the archangel, and with the trump of God: and the dead in Christ shall rise first.” 1 Thessalonians 4:16

Paul says “the Lord himself.” The One who first came in humility will return in glory. He who stood outside Lazarus’s tomb and commanded the dead to come forth will summon His people from every grave. Those who belong to Christ will not remain beneath the earth.

Not every believer, however, will be in the grave when Christ returns. Paul reveals:

“Behold, I shew you a mystery; We shall not all sleep, but we shall all be changed.” 1 Corinthians 15:51

The dead in Christ will rise and the living be changed, and the whole company of the redeemed will enter incorruptible life.

Paul continues:

“For this corruptible must put on incorruption, and this mortal must put on immortality.” 1 Corinthians 15:53

The body will not be discarded as though God had abandoned part of the humanity He created. It will be transformed. Redemption will extend to the whole person.

In the Christian cemetery, hope waits. The bodies of believers committed to the earth have not been forgotten by the God who made them. At the return of Christ, every apparent triumph of the grave over His people will be reversed.

Then the words of Scripture will be fulfilled: “Death is swallowed up in victory.” 1 Corinthians 15:54

The Last Enemy Destroyed

Paul calls death: “The last enemy that shall be destroyed…” 1 Corinthians 15:26

Death is an enemy, not a gentle guide towards fulfilment. It separates loved ones, ends earthly labour and returns the body to dust.

Across every generation, it has appeared to defeat the strong, silence the wise and reduce every human distinction to the level ground of the grave. But death is the last enemy, not the everlasting one.

Looking towards the resurrection of God’s people, Paul challenges death directly:

“O death, where is thy sting? O grave, where is thy victory?” 1 Corinthians 15:55

Paul has not underestimated death; he has understood Christ.

He immediately explains:

“The sting of death is sin; and the strength of sin is the law. But thanks be to God, which giveth us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ.” 1 Corinthians 15:56–57

Death drew its sting from sin, which brought humanity under judgment. Christ bore that judgment, answered sin and rose beyond death’s dominion.

The victory therefore does not arise from humanity’s courage, virtue or determination. God gives it through Jesus Christ our Lord.

Death may still enter the believer’s earthly experience, but it cannot annul his justification, sever his union with Christ or prevent his resurrection.

At Christ’s return, even its temporary presence will end. The last enemy will be destroyed.

God Shall Dwell with Them

God’s purpose is wider than the rescue of individuals from a ruined world. The Creator has not abandoned His creation.

John was permitted to see the future towards which redemption moves:

“And I saw a new heaven and a new earth: for the first heaven and the first earth were passed away.” Revelation 21:1

The final hope of Scripture is creation delivered from corruption and brought beneath the undisputed reign of God.

Scripture points to something greater still:

“Behold, the tabernacle of God is with men, and he will dwell with them, and they shall be his people, and God himself shall be with them, and be their God.” Revelation 21:3

This is the fulfilment towards which the whole story has been moving. In Eden, sin broke humanity’s fellowship with God.

At its centre is the greatest promise of eternity: God Himself dwelling with His people.

John continues:

“And God shall wipe away all tears from their eyes; and there shall be no more death, neither sorrow, nor crying, neither shall there be any more pain: for the former things are passed away.” Revelation 21:4

These words announce the complete reversal of the Fall. Death does not become less frequent or less painful. It disappears.

Revelation first records the final judgment described as “the second death” before announcing that within God’s renewed creation “there shall be no more death.” Evil is not carried untreated into eternity. Judgment is completed, mortality is abolished and nothing remains to disturb the fellowship of God with His redeemed people.

What began in Genesis as alienation, mortality and exile reaches its opposite in Revelation: reconciliation, incorruptible life and the presence of God.

The first pages of the Bible introduce death. The last pages announce death’s own funeral.

What entered through Adam’s disobedience finally disappears through the triumph of Jesus Christ. Fellowship lost in Eden is restored, and the enemy that humbled every generation exists no more.

Therefore We Do Not Fear

Believers may still experience fear, but death cannot determine their final condition. Its arrival need not govern how they live now.

Wealth cannot purchase immunity from death. Influence cannot negotiate with it, and learning cannot explain it away. The Gospel announces that Christ has overcome it.

This hope produced courage in the early Church. Men and women who no longer regarded death as ultimate were hard to intimidate.

Stephen displayed that confidence as stones fell upon him. He lifted his eyes towards heaven and declared:

“Behold, I see the heavens opened, and the Son of man standing on the right hand of God.” Acts 7:56

Even as his persecutors closed around him, Stephen’s final confidence rested upon the Christ who awaited him.

Earthly powers could wield imprisonment and execution, but the Church proclaimed a Lord whose victory placed even death beneath His authority. Christians could be killed, but not separated from Christ.

That confidence remains the inheritance of every believer. Christians do not pretend that death carries no sorrow. We still weep beside graves and mourn those whose earthly presence we miss.

But grief is no longer despair. Death often exercises its greatest power before it claims the body. It does so by persuading men and women to live in continual fear of its arrival. Entire lives may be shaped by that fear.

The Gospel breaks its tyranny. It does not promise that Christians will never die; it promises that death will never finally hold them.

This hope calls the believer to cherish life and to look after the people and duties God has entrusted to him. Every day offers opportunities to love, serve and honour commitments. Confidence in eternity gives these ordinary responsibilities greater weight.

We do not know how many days remain, but we are answerable for how we live them.

Freedom from the fear of death is freedom to live according to life’s purpose.

The Christian measures life less by its duration than by its direction. A life belonging to Christ cannot end in defeat because its future has already been secured by the One who declared:

“I am he that liveth, and was dead; and, behold, I am alive for evermore, Amen; and have the keys of hell and of death.” Revelation 1:18

We return to the governing declaration: “the wages of sin is death.”

But that is not the whole declaration.

“…but the gift of God is eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord.” Romans 6:23

Between those two halves stands the entire Gospel.

Sin paid its wages. Christ bore the judgment, entered death and rose beyond its power. The risen Lord now gives eternal life to those who receive Him and will return to bring that life to its completion.

The case has reached its conclusion. Death does not have the last word. Christ does.

Christians therefore live today in the eternal life secured by Jesus Christ, sustained by His grace and ready to meet Him, whether through death or at His promised return.

sections.title: Epilogue
sections.subtitle: The Gift Beyond the Wages
sections.html:
I began this book by speaking of my plans. I close it with people still depending upon me and responsibilities requiring time I cannot guarantee.

Tomorrow morning, alarms will sound, calendars will fill and millions of us will resume unfinished work. Contracts will be negotiated, businesses built, journeys begun and promises made in the reasonable expectation that life will continue.

I will be among those making plans. Medicine can treat illness, technology anticipate risk and wealth offer protection, but none has repealed mortality. Writing this book has made me aware that we prepare for tomorrow without possessing it.

That stops being abstract when we lose someone close. The public ceremonies end and ordinary responsibilities resume, but the absence remains. In my own case, there were conversations I still longed to have with my late father. A word of advice here, a little guidance there. Sometimes the instinct to telephone him came before the realisation that he was gone. The questions remained, but I could no longer hear his voice or tell him what was weighing on my mind.

His books remain, as do the convictions and responsibilities he entrusted to those who came after him. Through the Foundation’s literature work, I can help others encounter words he wrote. I cannot make that work a substitute for hearing, believing and living the truth myself.

Being his son does not settle my relationship with God. Preserving his Christian writings does not mean that their message has taken root in my own life. What I honour as his legacy must also test the confidence upon which I stand.

What do these conclusions require of the man who wrote them?

Legal practice has taught me to prepare thoroughly, anticipate objections and work towards a favourable outcome. These habits serve me well, but they can also encourage the belief that preparation brings every outcome within my control. Life reminds me otherwise.

A matter may remain unresolved after diligent work, and an enterprise may disappoint despite sound judgment. At such moments, I must ask what I expected success to secure: affirmation of my worth, protection against uncertainty or confidence about the future. The answer reveals where I placed my trust.

Writing about grace does not release me from dependence upon it. The truth I commend to others must also shape my response when events interrupt my plans.

Scripture speaks within these ordinary uncertainties. It invites us, having understood why we die, to receive the reconciliation Christ has accomplished and to enter fellowship with God.

Paul writes:

“Now then we are ambassadors for Christ, as though God did beseech you by us: we pray you in Christ’s stead, be ye reconciled to God.” 2 Corinthians 5:20

I cannot ask the reader to respond without recognising that this invitation addresses me too. Sin is more than a disorder in society, a failure in someone else or a truth I can explain from Scripture. I must acknowledge its presence in my own life.

Each of us must make that acknowledgement. We cease relying upon our own righteousness, turn from sin and entrust ourselves to Jesus Christ. Professional standing, family heritage and familiarity with Christian teaching cannot answer for us; each must personally receive God’s gift.

Paul expresses that response plainly:

“That if thou shalt confess with thy mouth the Lord Jesus, and shalt believe in thine heart that God hath raised him from the dead, thou shalt be saved.” Romans 10:9

Confessing Christ as Lord brings our ambitions, relationships, possessions and time under His authority. His gift of eternal life shapes how we live now.

These responsibilities do not stop at this manuscript. As a lawyer, I owe clients sound judgment and faithful attention; as a husband and father, I owe my family more than the time work and ambition leave behind.

These duties often go unseen. A promise kept, an attentive conversation or an inconvenient duty fulfilled may reveal more about my lived faith than eloquent explanations.

Faithful attention means understanding what a client is asking, explaining an unwelcome answer plainly and resisting the temptation to promise an outcome I cannot control. These duties test the dependence I have commended throughout this book.

At home, attention means more than being present in the room. I must put aside a preoccupation, hear my wife fully and make room for my son’s questions without treating them as interruptions. Those closest to me should encounter the patience and care of which I write. Publication cannot bear witness to a faith my conduct leaves difficult for them to recognise.

Grace gives these responsibilities their setting. They are responses to God’s generosity, never means of placing Him under obligation. Eternal life cannot become another achievement by which I attempt to secure myself.

Outcomes matter. Illness troubles us, financial uncertainty requires judgment and bereavement leaves an absence no explanation can fill. Faith permits us to seek good outcomes while placing our ultimate confidence in Christ.

I still want time to see my family grow, serve them and complete worthwhile work. Christian hope lets me cherish these desires without expecting their fulfilment to provide what only God can give.

Author and reader therefore stand together. Have we received the life offered through Jesus Christ, or have we merely become familiar with its description? Where does our confidence rest when the things we have built cannot promise another morning?

Those questions need an answer now. We cannot reserve reconciliation with God for a future whose arrival we do not control. His gift calls for a response while we have life in which to receive it.

If earthly life ends before Christ returns, the believer’s hope is to be with Him and await the resurrection He has promised. If He returns while we remain alive, our hope is to be transformed and gathered to Him. In either case, our future rests upon the Lord who entered death and rose beyond its dominion.

I close this book with responsibilities still unfinished and questions about tomorrow still unanswered. I intend to keep working, planning and caring for those entrusted to me. What must change is the confidence from which I do so.

The wages have been examined and the gift proclaimed. Their meaning now passes from these pages into the ordinary morning that may follow.

My prayer is for our Father, who knows our tomorrow, to grant us another day and, by His Holy Spirit, guide us to receive it with gratitude and pursue our plans faithfully before Him. May the Spirit keep our hope rooted in the eternal life the Father gives through Jesus Christ, whatever remains unfinished when our days on earth come to an end. Amen.

That gift of eternal life through Jesus Christ is the hope I commend to you, and His grace is the ground upon which I too must stand.

sections.title: Appendix I
sections.subtitle: Key Scriptures on Sin, Death and Redemption
sections.html:
The passages below are grouped by the book’s principal themes to support personal study, reflection and discussion.

Read each passage within its surrounding chapter before considering its connection to the enquiry. The annotations identify its relevance without replacing the biblical text or implying that every passage addresses every aspect of the theme.

I. The Entrance of Sin and Death

Genesis 2:15–17 God’s provision, command to Adam and warning concerning death.

Genesis 3:1–24 Temptation, disobedience, shame, judgment, promise and expulsion from Eden.

Genesis 3:22–24 The Tree of Life and humanity’s exclusion from access to it.

Genesis 5:24; Hebrews 11:5 Enoch taken by God without experiencing death.

2 Kings 2:11 Elijah taken up into heaven by a whirlwind.

Psalm 51:5 David’s confession concerning sin from the beginning of his life, relevant to the discussion of humanity’s fallen condition.

Ecclesiastes 3:1–2 Birth and death within the seasons of earthly life.

II. Sin, Death and Human Responsibility

Deuteronomy 24:16; Ezekiel 18:20 Personal accountability for wrongdoing. Read alongside Romans 5, while distinguishing their treatment of individual culpability from Paul’s argument concerning Adam.

Romans 3:10–23 Humanity’s unrighteousness and universal need for God’s saving provision.

Romans 5:12–21 Sin, condemnation and death through Adam; righteousness, grace and life through Christ.

Romans 5:14 Death reigning even over those whose sins did not take the precise form of Adam’s transgression.

Romans 6:15–23 Masters, servants and obedience: the context of Paul’s contrast between wages and gift.

James 1:14–15 Desire, temptation, sin and death.

III. God’s Promise of Redemption

Genesis 3:15 Enmity between the serpent and the woman’s seed, understood within the wider Christian reading of Scripture as an initial promise of redemption.

Genesis 12:1–3 God’s promises to Abraham, including blessing for all families of the earth.

Exodus 12 The Passover: God’s appointed protection amid judgment and Israel’s departure from bondage. Compare 1 Corinthians 5:7 for its New Testament connection to Christ.

Leviticus 16 The Day of Atonement and God’s provision for Israel’s covenant worship.

Isaiah 53 The suffering Servant who bears the sins of others.

Jeremiah 31:31–34 The promised New Covenant, forgiveness and God’s Law written within His people.

IV. Jesus Christ Our Redeemer

John 1:1–18 The eternal Word, His deity and His becoming flesh.

Matthew 1:21–23 The birth of Jesus, His saving mission and the declaration of Emmanuel.

Romans 3:25–26 Christ’s propitiatory work, God’s forbearance concerning former sins and the demonstration of His righteousness.

Hebrews 9:15 Christ’s death redeeming transgressions committed under the first covenant.

Hebrews 2:14–18 Christ’s shared humanity, His death and His merciful ministry as High Priest.

Philippians 2:5–11 Christ’s humility, obedience and exaltation.

Colossians 1:13–20 The supremacy of the Son and reconciliation through the blood of His Cross.

V. The Cross and the Resurrection

Matthew 27 The condemnation, Crucifixion and burial of Jesus.

John 19:30 Christ’s declaration: “It is finished.”

Luke 24 The empty tomb, encounters with the risen Christ and His explanation of the Scriptures.

Acts 2:22–36 Peter’s proclamation of Christ’s death, Resurrection and exaltation.

Romans 6:9 The risen Christ, over whom death has no further dominion.

1 Corinthians 15 Apostolic testimony, Christ as firstfruits and the promised resurrection of His people.

VI. Salvation by Grace Through Faith

John 3:1–21 The new birth, God’s gift of His Son and eternal life through believing in Him.

Romans 5:1–11 Justification by faith, peace with God and reconciliation through Christ.

Romans 8 Freedom from condemnation, life in the Spirit and awaited bodily redemption.

Ephesians 2:1–10 Salvation by grace through faith, with good works as its appointed fruit.

James 2:14–26 The challenge to a profession of faith without works. Consider James’s examples alongside Paul’s account of grace and faith.

Titus 3:3–7 Salvation according to God’s mercy, renewal by the Holy Spirit and justification by grace.

VII. The Christian Life

John 14–16 Fellowship with Christ and the promised ministry of the Holy Spirit.

1 Corinthians 12:12–27 Believers as members of one body, sharing responsibility and care.

Galatians 5:16–26 Walking in the Spirit and the fruit He produces.

Galatians 6:1–2 Gentle restoration of those who fall and the bearing of one another’s burdens.

Ephesians 4:15–16 Growth into Christ through the shared life and contribution of His body.

Philippians 1:20–26 Service in earthly life and the hope of being with Christ after death.

Philippians 2:12–13 The believer’s obedience and God’s work within.

1 Thessalonians 5:16–24 Rejoicing, prayer, thanksgiving and sanctification.

VIII. Resurrection and the Believer’s Future Hope

John 5:28–29 The resurrection of life and the resurrection of judgment.

John 11:17–44 Christ’s declaration that He is the resurrection and the life, followed by the raising of Lazarus.

1 Corinthians 15:51–54 Transformation into incorruptibility: not all shall sleep, but all shall be changed.

1 Thessalonians 4:13–18 Christ’s return, the resurrection of the dead in Christ and the gathering of living believers with them.

Revelation 20:11–15 Final judgment and the second death.

Revelation 21–22 Renewed creation, the abolition of death and God dwelling with His people.

IX. The Assurance of Eternal Life

John 10:27–30 Christ’s sheep, their following Him and His promise of eternal life.

Romans 8:31–39 The believer’s confidence in God’s saving action and love through Christ.

1 John 5:11–13 Eternal life in the Son and the assurance given to those who believe in Him.

The Central Verse

“For the wages of sin is death; but the gift of God is eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord.” Romans 6:23

This verse governs the enquiry. The passages gathered here illuminate its contrast without making every biblical use of death identical.

As you study, distinguish what each passage expressly states from conclusions drawn by reading it alongside others. Consider how its testimony contributes to the whole account: humanity’s fallen condition, personal responsibility, God’s redemptive provision and the life He gives through His Son.

The aim is to return to Romans 6:23 with fuller understanding of both the tragedy disclosed by the wages and the hope announced in the gift.

sections.title: Appendix II
sections.subtitle: Questions for Personal Reflection and Group Discussion
sections.html:
These questions support personal reflection, Bible study groups and church discussions. Take them at a thoughtful pace, returning to the relevant passages rather than relying upon the book’s explanations alone.

In a group, allow room for uncertainty and honest disagreement. Distinguish what Scripture expressly states from interpretation or inference. No participant should feel obliged to disclose private grief, personal failures or family circumstances.

Questions for Personal Reflection

1.     How has this enquiry changed my understanding of death?

2.     What responsibility or conversation have I been postponing as though tomorrow were guaranteed?

3.     Where am I resisting God’s authority or insisting upon my own terms?

4.     Am I relying upon morality, religious activity, achievement or reputation for acceptance before God?

5.     What does the Incarnation reveal about God’s willingness to draw near to humanity?

6.     How does Christ’s complete humanity deepen my confidence in approaching Him with weakness and need?

7.     Why does Christ’s sinlessness matter to my understanding of His death?

8.     What does the Cross reveal about the seriousness of my sin and God’s provision for it?

9.     How does Christ’s Resurrection shape my hope beyond the grave?

10.  Have I personally responded to God’s gift through repentance and faith in Jesus Christ? What questions or hesitations remain?

11.  Where can I recognise the Spirit’s transforming work in my life, and where do I need correction?

12.  When I fail, does the recognition of sin lead me towards confession, or does despair make me afraid to return to Christ?

13.  What costly act of obedience is before me: acknowledging an error, honouring a promise, repairing a relationship or giving someone proper attention?

14.  How might readiness to meet Christ change the way I approach today’s responsibilities and uncertain outcomes?

15.  With whom might I share the hope explored in this book, listening respectfully to their questions?

Questions for Group Discussion

1.     How do biological explanations of death and the biblical account of humanity’s mortal condition address different questions?

2.     How do Enoch, Elijah and Paul’s declaration “We shall not all sleep” qualify the claim that every person must experience physical death?

3.     What does Genesis expressly describe after Adam and Eve’s disobedience? Which further conclusions depend upon the wider testimony of Scripture?

4.     How should we distinguish physical death, alienation from God and final judgment without treating every use of death as identical?

5.     How can Paul’s teaching concerning Adam be held together with personal responsibility? Why does an individual’s death not prove that a particular personal offence caused it?

6.     What did promise, covenant, Law, sacrifice and prophecy contribute to God’s unfolding redemptive purpose?

7.     How do Romans 3:25–26 and Hebrews 9:15 connect those who trusted God before Calvary with Christ’s saving work?

8.     Why does the book argue that the Redeemer must be truly God, completely human and without sin?

9.     What moral objection arises when the innocent suffers for the guilty? Consider why consent alone is insufficient before examining Christ’s representative identity and God’s own provision in Him.

10.  How do sacrifice, ransom, reconciliation and victory illuminate complementary aspects of the Cross?

11.  What testimony do the apostles present concerning Christ’s bodily Resurrection? How does that Resurrection differ from earlier restorations to mortal life?

12.  How should grace as the source, Christ’s work as the ground, faith as reception and good works as fruit be distinguished? Discuss repentance, confession and baptism within that order.

13.  Why do Christians ordinarily still die, and how can resurrection hope coexist with grief and fear?

14.  How should a church practise correction, repentance and care when a member fails or a household suffers? What would grace require in a concrete example?

15.  Why does the final Christian hope include bodily resurrection, renewed creation and God dwelling with His people?

Final Reflection

Return to the declaration from which this enquiry began:

“For the wages of sin is death; but the gift of God is eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord.” Romans 6:23

Which question still needs careful study? What response should follow from what you now understand?

The purpose of this enquiry reaches beyond knowing more about God. It calls us to know Him, trust Him and live faithfully in the life He gives.

Until faith becomes sight.

sections.title: Appendix III
sections.subtitle: Further Reading and Select Bibliography
sections.html:
These works include sources referenced in the book and selected further reading. Brief notes locate attributed ideas or indicate a work’s relevance. Book, chapter and section references remain useful across editions.

Holy Scripture

The Holy Bible: King James Version. First published in 1611. The translation used throughout this book.

Early Christian Thought

Athanasius. On the Incarnation. Translated by John Behr. Yonkers, NY: St Vladimir’s Seminary Press, 2011.
See sections 7–10 on the Creator’s restoration of humanity and 20, 26–27 on death and Resurrection.

Augustine of Hippo. Confessions. Translated by Henry Chadwick. Oxford: Oxford University Press, 1991.
See X.29.40 for the prayer concerning grace and obedience discussed in Chapter Eleven.

Augustine of Hippo. On Grace and Free Will. In Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, First Series, Vol. 5. Edited by Philip Schaff. Buffalo, NY: Christian Literature Publishing Company, 1887.
See chapters 12–13 on grace preceding merit and 16–17 on God’s work within obedience.

Augustine of Hippo. Expositions on the Psalms. In Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, First Series, Vol. 8. Edited by Philip Schaff. Buffalo, NY: Christian Literature Publishing Company, 1888.
See Psalm 61, section 3—Psalm 60 in Augustine’s numbering—for Christ’s temptation and victory.

Augustine of Hippo. The City of God against the Pagans. Edited and translated by R. W. Dyson. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1998.
Further reading on sin, death and Christian hope.

Gregory of Nazianzus. Select Letters. Translated by Charles Gordon Browne and James Edward Swallow. In Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Second Series, Vol. 7. Edited by Philip Schaff and Henry Wace. Buffalo, NY: Christian Literature Publishing Company, 1894.
Epistle 101, to Cledonius, defends Christ’s complete humanity, including a human mind.

Irenaeus. Against Heresies. Translated by Alexander Roberts and William Rambaut. In Ante-Nicene Fathers, Vol. 1. Edited by Alexander Roberts and James Donaldson. Buffalo, NY: Christian Literature Publishing Company, 1885.
See III.18.1–2 on humanity’s restoration in Christ, the last Adam.

Reformation and Classic Christian Theology

Calvin, John. Institutes of the Christian Religion. Edited by John T. McNeill. Translated by Ford Lewis Battles. 2 vols. Philadelphia: Westminster Press, 1960.
See III.1.1 on the Spirit uniting believers to Christ; II.7.6–8 on the Law exposing sin.

The Cross and Redemption

Morris, Leon. The Apostolic Preaching of the Cross. 3rd revised ed. Grand Rapids, MI: Eerdmans, 1965.
A study of redemption, sacrifice, reconciliation and propitiation.

Murray, John. Redemption Accomplished and Applied. Grand Rapids, MI: Eerdmans, 1955.
Distinguishes Christ’s completed work from its application to believers.

Sproul, R. C. The Holiness of God. Wheaton, IL: Tyndale House Publishers, 1985.
Further reading on holiness, worship and grace.

Stott, John R. W. The Cross of Christ. Leicester: Inter-Varsity Press, 1986.
See chapter 6, “The Self-Substitution of God,” for the argument discussed in Chapter Seven.

Christian Life and Grace

Lewis, C. S. Mere Christianity. London: Geoffrey Bles, 1952.
See Book III, chapter 10, “Hope,” on eternal expectation and present responsibility.

Packer, J. I. Knowing God. London: Hodder & Stoughton, 1973.
Explores knowing God personally and responding to His character.

Resurrection and Christian Hope

Cullmann, Oscar. Christ and Time: The Primitive Christian Conception of Time and History. 3rd revised ed. Translated by Floyd V. Filson. London: SCM Press, 1962.
See Part I, chapter 5, for decisive victory and awaited fulfilment, discussed in Chapter Ten.

Hoekema, Anthony A. The Bible and the Future. Grand Rapids, MI: Eerdmans, 1979.
A systematic study of Christian hope and the kingdom’s present and future dimensions.

Wright, N. T. The Resurrection of the Son of God. Christian Origins and the Question of God, Vol. 3. Minneapolis, MN: Fortress Press, 2003.
See Parts I–II on ancient resurrection expectations and Paul’s teaching concerning bodily resurrection.

sections.title: Appendix IV
sections.subtitle: Summary Scripture Guide
sections.html:
This index lists selected passages by biblical book, complementing Appendix I’s thematic guide.

Old Testament

Genesis: 2:15–17 — God’s provision, command and warning of death; 3:1–24 — The Fall, judgment, promise and exile; 3:15 — The promise understood in relation to redemption; 3:22–24 — Exclusion from the Tree of Life; 5:24 — Enoch taken by God; 12:1–3 — God’s promises to Abraham.

Exodus: 12 — Passover and deliverance from Egypt.

Leviticus: 16 — The Day of Atonement; 17:11 — Blood and God’s provision for atonement.

Deuteronomy: 24:16 — Personal responsibility for wrongdoing.

2 Kings: 2:11 — Elijah taken up into heaven.

Psalms: 23 — Confidence in God amid death’s shadow; 51:5 — David’s confession concerning sin from the beginning of his life.

Proverbs: 17:15 — The injustice of justifying the wicked and condemning the righteous.

Ecclesiastes: 3:1–2 — A time to be born and a time to die.

Isaiah: 53 — The suffering Servant who bears the sins of others.

Jeremiah: 31:31–34 — The promised New Covenant, inward renewal and forgiveness.

Ezekiel: 18:20 — Personal accountability for sin.

New Testament

Matthew: 1:21–23 — The Saviour’s birth; 4:1–11 — Christ’s obedience under temptation; 6:9 — Prayer to our Father; 27 — The Crucifixion and burial.

Luke: 15:24 — Estrangement and restoration described as death and life; 23:39–43 — The criminal’s appeal and Christ’s promise; 24 — The Resurrection.

John: 1:1–18 — The eternal Word became flesh; 1:29 — The Lamb of God; 3:1–21 — New birth and eternal life; 3:36 — Eternal life as a present possession; 5:28–29 — Resurrection to life or judgment; 8:29 — Christ’s obedience to the Father; 10:17–18 — His voluntary laying down of His life; 10:27–30 — Christ’s sheep and His promise of life; 11:17–44 — Grief, resurrection and life; 14–16 — Christ’s promises and the Holy Spirit; 17:3 — Eternal life as knowing God through Christ; 19:30 — “It is finished.”

Acts: 1:1–11 — The risen Christ, His commission and Ascension; 2:22–36 — Peter’s proclamation of Christ’s death, Resurrection and exaltation; 2:38 — Repentance, baptism and the promised Spirit; 4:12 — Salvation through Christ; 7:54–60 — Stephen’s martyrdom.

Romans: 3:10–23 — Humanity’s unrighteousness; 3:25–26 — Propitiation, former sins and God’s righteousness; 4:3 — Abraham’s faith; 5:1–11 — Justification and reconciliation; 5:12–21 — Adam and Christ; 6:9 — Christ dies no more; 6:15–23 — Masters, obedience, wages and gift; 8:1–39 — Life in the Spirit, bodily redemption and assurance; 10:9–13 — Faith, confession and salvation.

1 Corinthians: 5:7 — Christ our Passover; 12:12–27 — Believers as members of one body; 15 — Christ’s Resurrection and the believer’s hope; 15:51–54 — Resurrection and transformation into incorruptible life.

2 Corinthians: 3:18 — Transformation by the Spirit; 5:17–21 — New creation, reconciliation and Christ’s work for sinners.

Galatians: 4:4 — The Son sent in the fullness of time; 5:16–26 — Walking in the Spirit; 6:1–2 — Gentle restoration and shared burdens.

Ephesians: 1:13 — Believing the Gospel and being sealed with the Spirit; 2:1–10 — Salvation by grace through faith and its fruit; 2:18 — Access to the Father through Christ by the Spirit; 4:15–16 — Shared growth into Christ.

Philippians: 1:20–26 — Life, death and fellowship with Christ; 2:5–11 — Christ’s humility, obedience and exaltation; 2:12–13 — Obedience through God’s work within.

Colossians: 1:13–20 — Christ’s supremacy and reconciling work; 2:9 — The fullness of the Godhead dwelling bodily in Christ.

1 Thessalonians: 4:13–18 — Grief, hope and Christ’s return; 5:16–24 — Prayer, thanksgiving and sanctification.

1 Timothy: 2:5 — Christ the Mediator.

2 Timothy: 1:10 — Christ’s victory over death and the revelation of life and immortality.

Titus: 3:3–7 — Salvation through God’s mercy.

Hebrews: 2:14–18 — Christ’s humanity and victory over the devil; 4:14–16 — Our High Priest and access to grace; 9:15 — Redemption of transgressions under the first covenant; 9:26–27 — Christ’s sacrifice, death and judgment; 10:1–12 — Repeated sacrifices and Christ’s completed offering; 11:5 — Enoch translated without seeing death; 11:13 — Faith before the promises’ fulfilment.

James: 1:14–15 — Desire, sin and death; 2:14–26 — Living faith and works.

1 Peter: 2:21–25 — Christ’s sinlessness, example and bearing of our sins.

2 Peter: 3:18 — Growth in grace and the knowledge of Christ.

1 John: 4:10 — God’s love and Christ’s propitiatory work; 5:11–13 — Eternal life in the Son and assurance.

Revelation: 1:17–18 — Christ’s authority over hell and death; 20:11–15 — Final judgment and the second death; 21–22 — Renewed creation, God’s presence and the end of death.
